papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language model (LLM) pruning have shown state-of-the-art (SotA) compression results in post-training and retraining-free settings while maintaining high predictive performance. However, previous research mainly considered calibrating based on English text, despite the multilingual nature of modern LLMs and their frequent use in non-English languages. This analysis paper conducts an in-depth investigation of the performance and internal representation changes associated with pruning multilingual language models for monolingual applications. We present the first comprehensive empirical study, comparing different calibration languages for pruning multilingual models across diverse languages, tasks, models, and SotA pruning techniques. We further analyze the latent subspaces, pruning masks, and individual neurons within pruned models. Our results reveal that while calibration on the target language effectively retains perplexity and yields high signal-to-noise ratios, it does not consistently improve downstream task performance. Further analysis of internal representations at three different levels highlights broader limitations of current pruning approaches: While they effectively preserve dominant information like language-specific features, this is insufficient to counteract the loss of nuanced, language-agnostic features that are crucial for knowledge retention and reasoning.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission
papers.research_question: How can we perform soft context compression more effectively by addressing the structural limitations (representation overwriting and uncoordinated allocation) of existing LLM-as-a-compressor methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a new paradigm for soft context compression by formulating it as explicit information transmission over frozen LLM hidden states, which decouples compression from internal self-attention dynamics and enables coordinated depth-wise and width-wise transmission for more effective and robust compression.
papers.conclusion: ComprExIT presents a new, effective paradigm for soft context compression via explicit information transmission over frozen LLM states, mitigating distribution shift and enabling coordinated allocation, as demonstrated by superior performance across diverse QA benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
ComprExIT consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art soft compression methods (ICAE, 500x, Activation Beacon) across six in-domain QA benchmarks.
ComprExIT matches or even surpasses the performance of an uncompressed, prompt-tuned baseline on several datasets, indicating effective compression with minimal information loss.
The method shows strong generalization and robustness, maintaining performance gains in out-of-domain evaluations and when trained only with a next-token prediction objective.
Ablation studies confirm that both coordinated allocation (width-wise transmission) and layer aggregation (depth-wise transmission) are critical components for the method's success.
Analysis reveals that ComprExIT's compression tokens exhibit low inter-slot correlation and a higher effective rank in allocation compared to prior methods, indicating more efficient and coordinated information usage.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to relatively smaller LLMs (1B to 3B parameters), a context length of 512 tokens, and a fixed compression ratio (x4) due to computational resource constraints.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models with various compression ratios and context lengths.
Investigating the method on other model families beyond the tested LLMs.
Exploring more design choices within the proposed explicit information transmission paradigm.
papers.abstract: Long-context inference with Large Language Models (LLMs) is costly due to quadratic attention and growing key-value caches, motivating context compression. In this work, we study soft context compression, where a long context is condensed into a small set of continuous representations. Existing methods typically re-purpose the LLM itself as a trainable compressor, relying on layer-by-layer self-attention to iteratively aggregate information. We argue that this paradigm suffers from two structural limitations: (i) progressive representation overwriting across layers (ii) uncoordinated allocation of compression capacity across tokens. We propose ComprExIT (Context Compression via Explicit Information Transmission), a lightweight framework that formulates soft compression into a new paradigm: explicit information transmission over frozen LLM hidden states. This decouples compression from the model's internal self-attention dynamics. ComprExIT performs (i) depth-wise transmission to selectively transmit multi-layer information into token anchors, mitigating progressive overwriting, and (ii) width-wise transmission to aggregate anchors into a small number of slots via a globally optimized transmission plan, ensuring coordinated allocation of information. Across six question-answering benchmarks, ComprExIT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art context compression methods while introducing only ~1% additional parameters, demonstrating that explicit and coordinated information transmission enables more effective and robust long-context compression.

papers.title: Efficient LLMs with AMP: Attention Heads and MLP Pruning
papers.research_question: How can Large Language Models be efficiently compressed by pruning less critical attention heads and MLP neurons while maintaining performance and achieving inference speedups without specialized hardware?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AMP, a structured pruning method that uses activation magnitudes to identify and remove less important attention heads and MLP neurons, achieving state-of-the-art compression with minimal performance loss and practical inference speedups.
papers.conclusion: AMP is an efficient and effective structured pruning method that compresses LLMs with minimal performance loss, provides inference speedups, and aligns with Green AI principles by reducing computational costs.
papers.key_findings:
AMP outperforms existing structured pruning methods on commonsense reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to 1.49 percentage points higher average accuracy.
The method achieves up to 1.25x inference speedup without requiring specialized hardware.
A coherence check validates that AMP correctly identifies less important components; pruning the most important components instead causes severe performance degradation.
Pruning both attention heads and MLP neurons together yields better results than pruning only one component type.
The pruning process is computationally efficient, requiring only minutes on a consumer-grade GPU.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models (Phi-1.5 and Phi-2) exhibit a more pronounced performance drop after pruning compared to larger models, indicating greater sensitivity to compression.
Post-training fine-tuning is critical for performance recovery, but extending fine-tuning epochs does not significantly improve results, suggesting the need for larger datasets.
future_direction: Investigate the use of different pruning ratios for attention heads and MLP neurons.
Explore extending post-training on larger datasets to improve performance recovery after pruning.
papers.abstract: Deep learning drives a new wave in computing systems and triggers the automation of increasingly complex problems. In particular, Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced cognitive tasks, often matching or even surpassing human-level performance. However, their extensive parameters result in high computational costs and slow inference, posing challenges for deployment in resource-limited settings. Among the strategies to overcome the aforementioned challenges, pruning emerges as a successful mechanism since it reduces model size while maintaining predictive ability. In this paper, we introduce AMP: Attention Heads and MLP Pruning, a novel structured pruning method that efficiently compresses LLMs by removing less critical structures within Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). By projecting the input data onto weights, AMP assesses structural importance and overcomes the limitations of existing techniques, which often fall short in flexibility or efficiency. In particular, AMP surpasses the current state-of-the-art on commonsense reasoning tasks by up to 1.49 percentage points, achieving a 30% pruning ratio with minimal impact on zero-shot task performance. Moreover, AMP also improves inference speeds, making it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained environments. We confirm the flexibility of AMP on different families of LLMs, including LLaMA and Phi.

papers.title: Do Wide and Deep Networks Learn the Same Things? Uncovering How Neural Network Representations Vary with Width and Depth
papers.research_question: How do depth and width affect the learned representations of neural networks? Do wide and deep networks learn the same things?
papers.core_contribution: Wide and deep networks develop a block structure in their representations when overparameterized, which arises from preserving and propagating the first principal component. Representations outside the block structure are similar across architectures, but the block structure is unique to each model.
papers.conclusion: Width and depth have distinct effects on neural network representations and predictions, with the block structure being a characteristic of overparameterized models.
papers.key_findings:
Wide and deep networks exhibit a block structure in their hidden representations when overparameterized relative to the dataset.
The block structure arises from the preservation and propagation of the first principal component of the layer representations.
Representations outside the block structure are similar across different architectures and initializations, but the block structure is unique to each model.
Linear probe accuracy plateaus within the block structure, and some layers in the block can be pruned with minimal performance loss.
Wide and deep models make systematically different errors at the example and class levels, even when overall accuracy is similar.
papers.limitation: There remain open questions on how the block structure arises through training and how to use these insights for model design.
future_direction: Understanding how the block structure arises through training
Using insights on depth and width to inform optimal task-specific model design
papers.abstract: A key factor in the success of deep neural networks is the ability to scale models to improve performance by varying the architecture depth and width. This simple property of neural network design has resulted in highly effective architectures for a variety of tasks. Nevertheless, there is limited understanding of effects of depth and width on the learned representations. In this paper, we study this fundamental question. We begin by investigating how varying depth and width affects model hidden representations, finding a characteristic block structure in the hidden representations of larger capacity (wider or deeper) models. We demonstrate that this block structure arises when model capacity is large relative to the size of the training set, and is indicative of the underlying layers preserving and propagating the dominant principal component of their representations. This discovery has important ramifications for features learned by different models, namely, representations outside the block structure are often similar across architectures with varying widths and depths, but the block structure is unique to each model. We analyze the output predictions of different model architectures, finding that even when the overall accuracy is similar, wide and deep models exhibit distinctive error patterns and variations across classes.

papers.title: Measuring Representational Robustness of Neural Networks Through Shared Invariances
papers.research_question: How can we measure the extent to which two neural networks share representational invariances?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STIR, a measure of shared invariances between neural networks, and uses it to gain insights into how shared invariances vary with weight initialization, architecture, loss functions, and training dataset.
papers.conclusion: STIR is a useful measure for studying shared invariances and provides insights into how design choices affect robustness, with potential applications in safety-critical model updates.
papers.key_findings:
STIR can capture shared invariances where existing similarity measures like CKA fail.
Shared invariances are higher in earlier layers and decrease in later layers for models trained with vanilla loss, but adversarial training leads to high shared invariances across all layers.
Models with residual connections have higher shared invariances among themselves.
Different adversarial training methods (AT, TRADES, MART) achieve robustness in different ways, leading to only mild shared invariances between them.
Adding more training data increases shared invariances between model updates.
papers.limitation:
STIR requires generating IRIs, which can be computationally expensive.
STIR is defined for a given reference model and input distribution, and may not generalize to other distributions.
The study is limited to image classification tasks.
future_direction: Extend STIR to other modalities and tasks.
Use STIR to study invariances in self-supervised learning.
Use STIR during training to encourage one model to follow similar invariances to another.
papers.abstract: A major challenge in studying robustness in deep learning is defining the set of ``meaningless'' perturbations to which a given Neural Network (NN) should be invariant. Most work on robustness implicitly uses a human as the reference model to define such perturbations. Our work offers a new view on robustness by using another reference NN to define the set of perturbations a given NN should be invariant to, thus generalizing the reliance on a reference ``human NN'' to any NN. This makes measuring robustness equivalent to measuring the extent to which two NNs share invariances, for which we propose a measure called STIR. STIR re-purposes existing representation similarity measures to make them suitable for measuring shared invariances. Using our measure, we are able to gain insights into how shared invariances vary with changes in weight initialization, architecture, loss functions, and training dataset. Our implementation is available at: \url{https://github.com/nvedant07/STIR}.

papers.title: Interpretability-Aware Pruning for Efficient Medical Image Analysis
papers.research_question: How can interpretability techniques be used to guide pruning of neural networks to reduce model complexity while preserving predictive performance and transparency in medical image analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability-guided pruning framework that leverages attribution methods to prune neurons, achieving high compression rates with minimal accuracy loss for medical image models.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-guided pruning offers an effective pathway to building lightweight, interpretable, and potentially more robust AI systems for deployment in high-stakes domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability-guided pruning enables high model compression while maintaining accuracy within a 5% margin across datasets and architectures.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) show exceptional robustness to pruning, preserving performance even beyond 65-80% pruning rates.
Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) consistently achieves the highest pruning thresholds with the lowest accuracy drop compared to DL-Backtrace and Integrated Gradients.
Clustering-based sampling for importance computation outperforms confidence-based and random sampling, providing more robust pruning results.
Pruning can sometimes improve accuracy by removing neurons with negative or noisy influence, enhancing generalization.
future_direction: Pruning pre-trained models using region-specific, representative data to improve generalization at deployment.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has driven significant advances in medical image analysis, yet its adoption in clinical practice remains constrained by the large size and lack of transparency in modern models. Advances in interpretability techniques such as DL-Backtrace, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, and Integrated Gradients make it possible to assess the contribution of individual components within neural networks trained on medical imaging tasks. In this work, we introduce an interpretability-guided pruning framework that reduces model complexity while preserving both predictive performance and transparency. By selectively retaining only the most relevant parts of each layer, our method enables targeted compression that maintains clinically meaningful representations. Experiments across multiple medical image classification benchmarks demonstrate that this approach achieves high compression rates with minimal loss in accuracy, paving the way for lightweight, interpretable models suited for real-world deployment in healthcare settings.

papers.title: Understanding Neural Networks through Representation Erasure
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural network decisions by analyzing the effects of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a general methodology for interpreting neural network decisions by erasing parts of the representation and analyzing the effects, which provides explanations for model behavior and enables error analysis.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology offers interpretable explanations for neural model decisions and provides a way to conduct error analysis, which can benefit a wide variety of models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies important word-vector dimensions for linguistic feature classification and shows how importance distributes across dimensions and layers.
In sentiment analysis, LSTM-based models are more sensitive to sentiment-indicative words than standard RNNs.
The method can identify words that confuse the model (negative importance) and reveal common failure patterns, such as sentiment words used in non-standard contexts.
A reinforcement learning approach can find minimal sets of words to erase to change model decisions, providing aspect-specific rationales.
Dropout training leads to more distributed importance across dimensions.
future_direction: Resolving the problems identified in error analysis (e.g., handling concessive sentences, irony, etc.) in sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to many natural language processing tasks, they come at the cost of interpretability. In this paper, we propose a general methodology to analyze and interpret decisions from a neural model by observing the effects on the model of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words. We present several approaches to analyzing the effects of such erasure, from computing the relative difference in evaluation metrics, to using reinforcement learning to erase the minimum set of input words in order to flip a neural model's decision. In a comprehensive analysis of multiple NLP tasks, including linguistic feature classification, sentence-level sentiment analysis, and document level sentiment aspect prediction, we show that the proposed methodology not only offers clear explanations about neural model decisions, but also provides a way to conduct error analysis on neural models.

papers.title: On the Power and Limitations of Random Features for Understanding Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the random features approach, which fixes some network components at random initialization, fully explain the empirical success of neural networks, particularly the learnability of simple functions like a single ReLU neuron?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while over-parameterized neural networks can learn low-degree polynomials via random features, the random features approach is inherently limited and cannot efficiently approximate a single ReLU neuron unless the network size or weight magnitudes are exponential in the input dimension.
papers.conclusion: The random features approach captures important aspects of neural network training but is insufficient to provide a complete explanation for their empirical success, as it fails to account for the learnability of simple functions like a single neuron.
papers.key_findings:
Over-parameterized one-hidden-layer neural networks can provably learn low-degree polynomials using standard stochastic gradient descent and random features.
Random features cannot approximate a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs unless the number of features or the magnitude of the weights is exponential in the input dimension.
Since single ReLU neurons are learnable with gradient-based methods, the random features approach cannot fully explain the empirical success of neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The positive result on learning polynomials requires the network size to be exponential in the degree of the polynomial.
The random features approach cannot fully explain polynomial-time learnability of neural networks, indicating that we are still far from a satisfying general explanation.
papers.abstract: Recently, a spate of papers have provided positive theoretical results for training over-parameterized neural networks (where the network size is larger than what is needed to achieve low error). The key insight is that with sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based methods will implicitly leave some components of the network relatively unchanged, so the optimization dynamics will behave as if those components are essentially fixed at their initial random values. In fact, fixing these explicitly leads to the well-known approach of learning with random features. In other words, these techniques imply that we can successfully learn with neural networks, whenever we can successfully learn with random features. In this paper, we first review these techniques, providing a simple and self-contained analysis for one-hidden-layer networks. We then argue that despite the impressive positive results, random feature approaches are also inherently limited in what they can explain. In particular, we rigorously show that random features cannot be used to learn even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs, unless the network size (or magnitude of the weights) is exponentially large. Since a single neuron is learnable with gradient-based methods, we conclude that we are still far from a satisfying general explanation for the empirical success of neural networks.

papers.title: TX-Ray: Quantifying and Explaining Model-Knowledge Transfer in\n (Un-)Supervised NLP
papers.research_question: How can we explain and quantify model knowledge transfer during (un-)supervised training in NLP? Specifically, how do self-supervised models build knowledge abstractions during pretraining, what knowledge subset is applied in zero-shot transfer to a new domain, and how does knowledge transfer 'backwards' from supervision labels into a pretrained model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TX-Ray, a method that modifies activation maximization to represent neurons as feature preference distributions, enabling the analysis, tracking, and quantification of knowledge transfer and adaptation during pretraining, zero-shot application, and supervised fine-tuning in NLP models.
papers.conclusion: TX-Ray enables explorative analysis of how knowledge is lost and added during supervision, how neurons overfit or generalize, and how pretraining builds knowledge abstractions, providing a simple yet nuanced method for model knowledge explainability in transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
TX-Ray can reveal how early stages of self-supervision automatically learn linguistic abstractions like parts-of-speech.
During zero-shot application, a pretrained encoder exhibits broad transfer, with 88.2% of neurons remaining 'shared' when applied to a new domain.
Supervision not only causes catastrophic forgetting but also adds new knowledge into previously unpreferred neurons.
TX-Ray-based pruning, similar to Lottery Ticket pruning, can improve test set generalization by removing 'avoided' neurons.
Supervision sparsifies neuron activations, leading to more peaked activation mass distributions compared to pretraining or zero-shot application.
future_direction: Use TX-Ray for more advanced transfer models and metrics.
papers.abstract:
While state-of-the-art NLP explainability (XAI) methods focus on explaining
per-sample decisions in supervised end or probing tasks, this is insufficient
to explain and quantify model knowledge transfer during (un-)supervised
training. Thus, for TX-Ray, we modify the established computer vision
explainability principle of 'visualizing preferred inputs of neurons' to make
it usable transfer analysis and NLP. This allows one to analyze, track and
quantify how self- or supervised NLP models first build knowledge abstractions
in pretraining (1), and then transfer these abstractions to a new domain (2),
or adapt them during supervised fine-tuning (3). TX-Ray expresses neurons as
feature preference distributions to quantify fine-grained knowledge transfer or
adaptation and guide human analysis. We find that, similar to Lottery Ticket
based pruning, TX-Ray based pruning can improve test set generalization and
that it can reveal how early stages of self-supervision automatically learn
linguistic abstractions like parts-of-speech.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: A Survey on Transformer Compression
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent compression methods for Transformer-based models, categorizing them into pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architecture design, and discusses their underlying principles and future directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that Transformer compression is crucial for practical deployment and provides a comprehensive categorization of methods, highlighting the importance of efficiency and the shared principles across domains, with several promising future research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer compression is a necessary step to implement large language/vision models on practical devices due to memory and computational constraints.
Compression methods for Transformers are primarily categorized into pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architecture design (e.g., Mamba, RetNet, RWKV).
The efficiency of compression methods is paramount for large models, as retraining on the entire dataset is usually impractical, making training-efficient methods like post-training compression preferable.
Compression methods for natural language processing and computer vision Transformers share similar underlying principles despite being different domains.
Future directions include combining different compression methods for extreme compression and developing more training-efficient pruning and quantization techniques.
future_direction: Combining different compression methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, distillation) for extreme compression.
Developing training-efficient compression methods, especially for pruning and quantization of large models.
Exploring the ceiling of pruning ratios for long contexts in large language models and making pruning more flexible, akin to continuous structural search.
papers.abstract: Transformer plays a vital role in the realms of natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), specially for constructing large language models (LLM) and large vision models (LVM). Model compression methods reduce the memory and computational cost of Transformer, which is a necessary step to implement large language/vision models on practical devices. Given the unique architecture of Transformer, featuring alternative attention and feedforward neural network (FFN) modules, specific compression techniques are usually required. The efficiency of these compression methods is also paramount, as retraining large models on the entire training dataset is usually impractical. This survey provides a comprehensive review of recent compression methods, with a specific focus on their application to Transformer-based models. The compression methods are primarily categorized into pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architecture design (Mamba, RetNet, RWKV, etc.). In each category, we discuss compression methods for both language and vision tasks, highlighting common underlying principles. Finally, we delve into the relation between various compression methods, and discuss further directions in this domain.

papers.title: When Does Pruning Benefit Vision Representations?
papers.research_question: How does neural network pruning affect model interpretability, object discovery capabilities, and alignment with human perceptual representations in vision models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that pruning affects vision models differently across architectures, with 'sweet spots' where sparse models can exhibit higher interpretability, downstream generalization, and human alignment, but these spots are highly dependent on network architecture and size.
papers.conclusion: Pruning affects vision representations across three key dimensions (interpretability, object discovery, human alignment), with specific configurations showing resilience or improvement, highlighting architectural differences and the existence of beneficial 'sweet spots'.
papers.key_findings:
For CNNs, interpretability and performance exhibit a negative correlation (higher interpretability with lower accuracy), while for Vision Transformers (ViTs) they are more positively correlated (lower interpretability with lower accuracy).
Pruning enhances object localization more in CNNs than in ViTs.
Smaller architectures (ResNet18, ViT-B/32) better preserve human-alignment than their larger counterparts (ResNet50, Swin) at high sparsity.
Sweet spots exist where both model accuracy and interpretability metrics simultaneously improve, such as at 15% sparsity for ResNet18 and 25.8% for ResNet50.
Pruning can lead to semantic drift in model predictions, with models focusing on spurious correlations (e.g., texture) as sparsity increases.
papers.limitation: The study focused on a limited set of models (two per architecture class: CNNs and ViTs) and applied a single pruning technique (LRR), evaluated using gradient-based explainability methods (IG, GradCAM, G-GradCAM).
future_direction: Investigate how pruning interacts with other desirable properties such as adversarial robustness and generalization capability.
Explore other compression techniques, including knowledge distillation, quantization, and low-rank decomposition.
Incorporate explainability-aware pruning approaches into the framework for comparison with magnitude-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pruning is widely used to reduce the complexity of deep learning models, but its effects on interpretability and representation learning remain poorly understood. This paper investigates how pruning influences vision models across three key dimensions: (i) interpretability, (ii) unsupervised object discovery, and (iii) alignment with human perception. We first analyze different vision network architectures to examine how varying sparsity levels affect feature attribution interpretability methods. Additionally, we explore whether pruning promotes more succinct and structured representations, potentially improving unsupervised object discovery by discarding redundant information while preserving essential features. Finally, we assess whether pruning enhances the alignment between model representations and human perception, investigating whether sparser models focus on more discriminative features similarly to humans. Our findings also reveal the presence of sweet spots, where sparse models exhibit higher interpretability, downstream generalization and human alignment. However, these spots highly depend on the network architectures and their size in terms of trainable parameters. Our results suggest a complex interplay between these three dimensions, highlighting the importance of investigating when and how pruning benefits vision representations.

papers.title: Representations as Language: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Interpretability
papers.research_question: What systematic structures emerge in the representations learned by transformers, and how do they relate to generalization and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework for interpretability that quantifies structure in representations, identifies two phases of training, and shows how representational structure relates to generalization and model size.
papers.conclusion: The linguistically-motivated approach helps characterize training dynamics and explain generalization, and suggests that intuitions from linguistics and cognitive science about good representations transfer to deep learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct phases of training: an initial phase of in-distribution learning where representations align with token and part-of-speech information, and a second phase where representations become robust to noise and compress.
Generalization performance improves during the second phase, linking generalization to robustness to noise.
Larger models compress their representations more than smaller models.
The proposed measures (information, variation, regularity, disentanglement) can predict which models will generalize best based on their representational structure.
papers.limitation:
Some results may be particular to the hyperparameters used for training.
The entropy estimation method is an approximation and makes minimal assumptions, but is invariant to linear transformations.
future_direction: Apply the analysis to large-scale translation tasks.
Extend the approach to other levels of abstraction and other models.
papers.abstract: Large scale neural models show impressive performance across a wide array of linguistic tasks. Despite this they remain, largely, black-boxes - inducing vector-representations of their input that prove difficult to interpret. This limits our ability to understand what they learn, and when the learn it, or describe what kinds of representations generalise well out of distribution. To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: Pruning of Convolutional Neural Networks Using Interpretability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
papers.research_question: How can the interpretability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks be leveraged to improve structural pruning of convolutional neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a structural pruning method for CNNs that uses a KAN layer as an interpretable bottleneck to assess filter importance based on B-spline coefficients, achieving better accuracy retention than traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed KAN-based pruning method provides a semantically justified criterion for network compression, enabling effective accuracy retention and inference speedup suitable for edge AI applications.
papers.key_findings:
The KAN-guided pruning method achieves 90.68% accuracy on CIFAR-10 after compression, outperforming magnitude-based pruning by 1.56% and knowledge distillation by 0.83%.
It reduces parameters from 11.2 million to 8.4 million (compression ratio 1.33×) with only 1.77% accuracy loss.
The method provides a 25% reduction in FLOPs, resulting in a 1.32× inference speedup on CPU.
Filter importance is quantified using the maximum weighted L2-norm of KAN spline coefficients, which correlates with semantic contribution.
Ablation studies show that a spline grid size of G=5 offers an optimal trade-off between accuracy and parameter efficiency.
future_direction: Extension to transformer architectures
Investigation of layer-wise importance criteria
Combination with quantization for further compression
papers.abstract: The paper addresses the pressing scientific and technical problem of over-parameterization in deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which hinders their effective deployment in Edge AI systems. Traditional compression methods, such as magnitude-based pruning, often remove functionally important components as they fail to account for the semantic contribution of filters to the final decision. This study proposes a novel structural pruning method leveraging the interpretability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN). A hybrid CNN-KAN architecture is developed, where the KAN layer acts as an "interpretable bottleneck," enabling the analysis of convolutional feature importance through learned B-spline coefficients. A mathematical importance criterion based on the maximum weighted L2-norm of spline coefficients is formalized. An iterative pruning algorithm with adaptive fine-tuning is developed. Experimental studies on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a compression ratio of 1.33× (reducing parameters from 11.2 million to 8.4 million) while maintaining an accuracy of 90.68%. This result outperforms classical pruning by 1.56% and is competitive with knowledge distillation methods

papers.title: Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can the cognitive mechanism of chunking be leveraged to interpret high-dimensional neural population activities in artificial neural networks? The paper tests the 'reflection hypothesis' that neural network activities reflect regularities in the data they are trained on.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework that uses the cognitive principle of chunking to identify recurring patterns (chunks) in neural embeddings, showing these chunks reflect data regularities and can causally influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The cognitive tendency for chunking can be leveraged to segment high-dimensional neural activity into recurring, interpretable chunks, revealing a structured reflection of the world within artificial neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
In simple RNNs trained on artificial sequences, hidden states reflect input regularities and can be extracted as interpretable chunks using discrete sequence chunking.
Extracted chunks in RNNs have a causal role: grafting these hidden states alters network predictions and can facilitate compositional learning.
In LLMs (LLaMA3-8B), neural population averaging can extract chunks corresponding to recurring words/concepts, with the extracted subpopulation activity serving as a classifier for the signal.
Unsupervised chunk discovery in LLM embeddings reveals chunks that correlate with abstract concepts like part-of-speech tags, suggesting they capture syntactic information.
The number and diversity of neural population chunks increase with the complexity and hierarchical structure of the input sequence, supporting the reflection hypothesis.
papers.limitation: The approach is an initial proof of concept and has limitations. Future work is needed to test it across different models, establish theoretical foundations, and refine chunk extraction methods.
future_direction: Test the reflection hypothesis across different models.
Establish theoretical foundations for the approach.
Refine chunk extraction methods, such as capturing multi-token chunks in unsupervised discovery.
Extend the framework toward nonparametric chunk discovery.
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging due to their high-dimensional, interacting components. Inspired by human cognition, which processes complex sensory data by chunking it into recurring entities, we propose leveraging this principle to interpret artificial neural population activities. Biological and artificial intelligence share the challenge of learning from structured, naturalistic data, and we hypothesize that the cognitive mechanism of chunking can provide insights into artificial systems. We first demonstrate this concept in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained on artificial sequences with imposed regularities, observing that their hidden states reflect these patterns, which can be extracted as a dictionary of chunks that influence network responses. Extending this to large language models (LLMs) like LLaMA, we identify similar recurring embedding states corresponding to concepts in the input, with perturbations to these states activating or inhibiting the associated concepts. By exploring methods to extract dictionaries of identifiable chunks across neural embeddings of varying complexity, our findings introduce a new framework for interpreting neural networks, framing their population activity as structured reflections of the data they process.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
papers.research_question: Does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? This paper challenges the view of representational optimism by comparing the internal representations of networks trained via open-ended search versus conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges representational optimism by introducing the Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) hypothesis, demonstrating that networks trained with conventional SGD can develop disorganized internal representations (FER) even when output performance is good, whereas networks from open-ended search can achieve more organized Unified Factored Representations (UFR).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) is a potential issue in conventional deep learning, raising questions about the adaptability of models trained via SGD, and that understanding and mitigating FER could be critical for the future of representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Networks trained with conventional SGD to produce a target image exhibit Fractured Entangled Representations (FER), where information for unitary concepts is split into disconnected, redundant pieces that become entangled.
Networks evolved through the open-ended Picbreeder process for the same output image exhibit Unified Factored Representations (UFR), where concepts are represented in a single, modular, and reusable manner.
Weight sweeps reveal that UFR networks allow for meaningful, human-recognizable variations (e.g., changing symmetry, stem angle) while respecting regularities, whereas FER networks produce deleterious, entangled changes that break regularities.
The path (curriculum) taken during learning influences the final representation; open-ended search discovers fundamental regularities (like symmetry) early, which are then elaborated upon, while conventional SGD takes a direct, greedy path.
The paper speculates that FER in large models may underlie challenges in generalization, creativity, and continual learning, and that the order in which concepts are learned is fundamental to the quality of the internal representation.
papers.limitation:
The study is conducted on a minimal, toy task (generating a single image) using CPPNs/MLPs, which is far simpler than large-scale models like LLMs.
The implications of FER for large models are speculative and based on analogy and limited examples of LLM behavior.
future_direction: Investigate FER in large models like LLMs and explore ways to mitigate it.
Study the impact of curricula and the ordering of concepts during training on the development of FER/UFR.
Explore alternative training algorithms and objectives (e.g., open-ended, novelty-seeking) that might lead to better internal representations.
papers.abstract: Much of the excitement in modern AI is driven by the observation that scaling up existing systems leads to better performance. But does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? While the representational optimist assumes it must, this position paper challenges that view. We compare neural networks evolved through an open-ended search process to networks trained via conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the simple task of generating a single image. This minimal setup offers a unique advantage: each hidden neuron's full functional behavior can be easily visualized as an image, thus revealing how the network's output behavior is internally constructed neuron by neuron. The result is striking: while both networks produce the same output behavior, their internal representations differ dramatically. The SGD-trained networks exhibit a form of disorganization that we term fractured entangled representation (FER). Interestingly, the evolved networks largely lack FER, even approaching a unified factored representation (UFR). In large models, FER may be degrading core model capacities like generalization, creativity, and (continual) learning. Therefore, understanding and mitigating FER could be critical to the future of representation learning.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: Isometric Representations in Neural Networks Improve Robustness
papers.research_question: Does enforcing isometric representations (preserving metric structure within classes) in neural networks improve robustness to adversarial attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Locally Isometric Layers (LILs), a method to enforce isometric representations within classes during training, which improves robustness to adversarial attacks while preserving topological structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper extends regularization methods by introducing a local isometry condition that maintains within-class structure across layers, leading to bounded gradients and improved robustness to adversarial attacks, as demonstrated on MNIST, and proposes stacking LILs for hierarchical classification.
papers.key_findings:
LILs can disentangle topologically entangled data while preserving within-class metric structure, unlike standard cross-entropy training.
Isometric mappings are 1-Lipschitz continuous, leading to bounded derivatives and improved robustness.
Empirical results on MNIST show increased robustness to FGSM and PGD attacks with the isometric loss term.
There is a trade-off between classification accuracy and robustness as the isometry weight (β) increases.
LILs can be stacked for hierarchical classification while preserving local structure.
papers.limitation:
Using large β values decreases classification performance, indicating a trade-off between performance and robustness.
It is unclear what the Lipschitz constant of a traditional cross-entropy trained neural network is.
The method has not been tested on more complex, hierarchically structured datasets like ImageNet.
future_direction: Investigate the trade-off between performance and robustness in more detail.
Apply the method to hierarchically structured datasets like ImageNet.
Explore applications in dimensionality reduction and data visualization.
papers.abstract: Artificial and biological agents cannon learn given completely random and unstructured data. The structure of data is encoded in the metric relationships between data points. In the context of neural networks, neuronal activity within a layer forms a representation reflecting the transformation that the layer implements on its inputs. In order to utilize the structure in the data in a truthful manner, such representations should reflect the input distances and thus be continuous and isometric. Supporting this statement, recent findings in neuroscience propose that generalization and robustness are tied to neural representations being continuously differentiable. In machine learning, most algorithms lack robustness and are generally thought to rely on aspects of the data that differ from those that humans use, as is commonly seen in adversarial attacks. During cross-entropy classification, the metric and structural properties of network representations are usually broken both between and within classes. This side effect from training can lead to instabilities under perturbations near locations where such structure is not preserved. One of the standard solutions to obtain robustness is to add ad hoc regularization terms, but to our knowledge, forcing representations to preserve the metric structure of the input data as a stabilising mechanism has not yet been studied. In this work, we train neural networks to perform classification while simultaneously maintaining within-class metric structure, leading to isometric within-class representations. Such network representations turn out to be beneficial for accurate and robust inference. By stacking layers with this property we create a network architecture that facilitates hierarchical manipulation of internal neural representations. Finally, we verify that isometric regularization improves the robustness to adversarial attacks on MNIST.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Experiments on Properties of Hidden Structures of Sparse Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can sparsity be achieved in neural networks through prior initialization, pruning, and during learning, and what is the relationship between the structure of neural networks and their performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides experimental insights into achieving sparsity via pruning, prior initialization, and learning, and demonstrates how structural properties of neural networks correlate with and can predict performance.
papers.conclusion: The experiments demonstrate that sparsity can be effectively achieved through pruning and prior design, and that structural properties of neural networks contain information that can be exploited for performance prediction and to guide architecture search.
papers.key_findings:
Magnitude class blinded pruning outperforms other pruning methods (random, class uniform, class distributed, Optimal Brain Damage) on feed-forward networks, achieving 97.5% accuracy on MNIST with 80% compression.
Pruning recurrent networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU) can achieve 60-80% sparsity without significant performance drop, and pruned models regain original performance within one to two re-training epochs.
LSTM and GRU can recover original performance even after 100% pruning of hidden-to-hidden weights.
Structural graph properties (e.g., number of nodes, edges, source nodes, closeness variance) correlate with model performance and can be used for architectural performance prediction.
A genetic neural architecture search enhanced with structural performance prediction achieves 82.4% accuracy on CIFAR10.
future_direction: Further research on how the bias from architectural priors or search strategies over architectures takes shape and its impact.
papers.abstract: Sparsity in the structure of Neural Networks can lead to less energy consumption, less memory usage, faster computation times on convenient hardware, and automated machine learning. If sparsity gives rise to certain kinds of structure, it can explain automatically obtained features during learning. We provide insights into experiments in which we show how sparsity can be achieved through prior initialization, pruning, and during learning, and answer questions on the relationship between the structure of Neural Networks and their performance. This includes the first work of inducing priors from network theory into Recurrent Neural Networks and an architectural performance prediction during a Neural Architecture Search. Within our experiments, we show how magnitude class blinded pruning achieves 97.5% on MNIST with 80% compression and re-training, which is 0.5 points more than without compression, that magnitude class uniform pruning is significantly inferior to it and how a genetic search enhanced with performance prediction achieves 82.4% on CIFAR10. Further, performance prediction for Recurrent Networks learning the Reber grammar shows an $R^2$ of up to 0.81 given only structural information.

papers.title: Improving Feature Attribution through Input-specific Network Pruning
papers.research_question: How can feature attribution be improved by pruning a neural network for a given single input to keep only neurons that highly contribute to the prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes input-specific network pruning to improve feature attribution, showing that gradients of the pruned network reflect global importance rather than local sensitivity, and the method outperforms existing gradient-based attribution methods across multiple benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Input-specific pruning improves feature attribution by making gradients reflect global importance, and the method is validated by theoretical connection to adversarial perturbations and extensive quantitative evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning neurons with low contribution changes gradients from reflecting local (noisy) importance to global importance.
The proposed PruneGrad method passes sanity checks and is sensitive to model parameter randomization.
PruneGrad outperforms other gradient-based methods in pixel perturbation and Remove-and-Retrain (ROAR) benchmarks.
The gradient of the pruned network is a sufficiently close solution to adversarial perturbations on the pruned network, providing a theoretical link.
Pruning helps uncover global features, and excessive pruning removes important features, degrading performance.
papers.abstract: Attributing the output of a neural network to the contribution of given input elements is a way of shedding light on the black-box nature of neural networks. Due to the complexity of current network architectures, current gradient-based attribution methods provide very noisy or coarse results. We propose to prune a neural network for a given single input to keep only neurons that highly contribute to the prediction. We show that by input-specific pruning, network gradients change from reflecting local (noisy) importance information to global importance. Our proposed method is efficient and generates fine-grained attribution maps. We further provide a theoretical justification of the pruning approach relating it to perturbations and validate it through a novel experimental setup. Our method is evaluated by multiple benchmarks: sanity checks, pixel perturbation, and Remove-and-Retrain (ROAR). These benchmarks evaluate the method from different perspectives and our method performs better than other methods across all evaluations.

papers.title: Compression supports low-dimensional representations of behavior across neural circuits
papers.abstract: Abstract Dimensionality reduction, a form of compression, can simplify representations of information to increase efficiency and reveal general patterns. Yet, this simplification also forfeits information, thereby reducing representational capacity. Hence, the brain may benefit from generating both compressed and uncompressed activity, and may do so in a heterogeneous manner across diverse neural circuits that represent low-level (sensory) or high-level (cognitive) stimuli. However, precisely how compression and representational capacity differ across the cortex remains unknown. Here we predict different levels of compression across regional circuits by using random walks on networks to model activity flow and to formulate rate-distortion functions, which are the basis of lossy compression. Using a large sample of youth ( n = 1, 040), we test predictions in two ways: by measuring the dimensionality of spontaneous activity from sensorimotor to association cortex, and by assessing the representational capacity for 24 behaviors in neural circuits and 20 cognitive variables in recurrent neural networks. Our network theory of compression predicts the dimensionality of activity ( t = 12.13, p < 0.001) and the representational capacity of biological ( r = 0.53, p = 0.016) and artificial ( r = 0.61, p < 0.001) networks. The model suggests how a basic form of compression is an emergent property of activity flow between distributed circuits that communicate with the rest of the network.

papers.title: Synaptic Pruning by Microglia in Epilepsy
papers.abstract: Structural and functional collapse of the balance between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) synapses, i.e., synaptic E/I balance, underlies the pathogeneses of various central nervous system (CNS) disorders. In epilepsy, the synaptic E/I balance tips toward excitation; thus, most of the existing epileptic remedies have focused on how to directly suppress the activity of neurons. However, because as many as 30% of patients with epilepsy are drug resistant, the discovery of new therapeutic targets is strongly desired. Recently, the roles of glial cells in epilepsy have gained attention because glial cells manipulate synaptic structures and functions in addition to supporting neuronal survival and growth. Among glial cells, microglia, which are brain-resident immune cells, have been shown to mediate inflammation, neuronal death and aberrant neurogenesis after epileptic seizures. However, few studies have investigated the involvement of synaptic pruning-one of the most important roles of microglia-in the epileptic brain. In this review, we propose and discuss the hypothesis that synaptic pruning by microglia is enhanced in the epileptic brain, drawing upon the findings of previous studies. We further discuss the possibility that aberrant synaptic pruning by microglia induces synaptic E/I imbalance, promoting the development and aggravation of epilepsy.

papers.title: A compressed code for memory discrimination
papers.abstract: The ability to discriminate similar visual stimuli has been used as an important index of memory function. This ability is widely thought to be supported by expanding the dimensionality of relevant neural codes, such that neural representations for the similar stimuli are maximally distinct, or "separated." An alternative hypothesis is that discrimination is supported by lossy compression of visual inputs, efficiently coding sensory information by discarding seemingly irrelevant details. A benefit of compression, relative to expansion, is that it allows the individual to efficiently retain fewer essential dimensions underlying stimulus variation-a process linked to higher-order visual processing-without hindering discrimination. Under the compression hypothesis, pattern separation is facilitated when more information from similar stimuli can be discarded, rather than preserving more information about distinct stimulus dimensions. We test the compression versus expansion hypotheses by predicting performance on the canonical mnemonic similarity task. First, we train neural networks to compress perceptual and semantic factors of stimuli, and measure lossiness of those representations using the mathematical framework underlying compression. Consistent with the compression hypothesis, and not the expansion hypothesis, we find that greater lossiness predicts the ease and performance of lure discrimination, particularly in later layers of convolutional neural networks shown to predict brain activity in the higher-order visual stream. We then empirically confirm these predictions across two sets of images, four behavioral datasets, and alternative metrics of lossiness.
