papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: Framework for Semantic Compression and Reconstruction in Large Language Models Using Layered Contextual Pruning
papers.research_question: How can large language models be compressed to reduce computational costs without compromising contextual and semantic fidelity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for semantic compression and reconstruction in LLMs using layered contextual pruning, balancing computational efficiency with linguistic coherence.
papers.conclusion: The semantic compression and reconstruction framework enables substantial reductions in model complexity while maintaining generative capabilities, supporting deployment in resource-constrained environments.
papers.key_findings:
Significant reductions in model parameters and inference time with minimal accuracy degradation up to certain compression ratios.
Reconstruction mechanisms effectively restore semantic fidelity, as shown by improved BLEU scores and perplexity metrics after fine-tuning.
Higher compression ratios lead to increased variability in perplexity and reduced vocabulary retention, especially in complex tasks like open-ended generation.
Layer-specific analysis shows that higher layers are more sensitive to pruning, with greater entropy reduction compared to lower layers.
The framework improves energy efficiency, with lower energy consumption during inference at higher compression levels.
papers.limitation:
Vulnerability to excessive noise can lead to performance degradation.
Scalability and generalizability across different architectures and deployment settings require further investigation.
future_direction: Develop adaptive strategies for dynamic resource allocation based on task complexity.
Optimize compression strategies for specific domains without exhaustive retraining.
Integrate semi-supervised learning or modular training paradigms to enhance efficiency.
papers.abstract: Compression techniques within deep transformer architectures have become an essential area of exploration to address growing computational demands while preserving high-quality generative outputs. By leveraging structured pruning methodologies and advanced reconstruction frameworks, the proposed approach reduces model complexity without compromising contextual and semantic fidelity. Iterative pruning cycles, combined with fine-tuning and attention redistribution mechanisms, ensure that linguistic coherence is maintained across varying compression levels. Results demonstrate significant gains in computational efficiency, with noticeable reductions in memory usage and inference latency, accompanied by relatively minimal degradation in task-specific accuracy. The integration of gradient alignment and multi-layer aggregation techniques provides a robust pathway for re-establishing disrupted contextual dependencies, ensuring adaptability in domain-specific tasks. Quantitative evaluations highlight the versatility of the proposed framework, as performance stability is observed across both general and specialized linguistic challenges. Further insights reveal that task complexity and noise levels significantly influence the trade-offs between compression ratios and generative quality. The innovative use of auxiliary loss functions and dynamic parameter adjustments underscores the importance of flexibility within compressed models. Energy efficiency evaluations highlight the broader implications of the methodology for sustainable AI deployments, particularly in resource-constrained environments. Together, the findings offer a comprehensive blueprint for enhancing the scalability and practicality of transformer-based architectures in modern computational linguistics.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Deep Representation Learning via Layerwise Feature Compression and Discrimination
papers.research_question: How do deep networks perform hierarchical feature learning across layers? Specifically, how do they transform input data into output across layers in classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that in deep linear networks, each layer progressively compresses within-class features at a geometric rate and discriminates between-class features at a linear rate, which also holds approximately in nonlinear networks.
papers.conclusion: Deep networks hierarchically compress and discriminate features across layers, providing a theoretical explanation for empirical observations of progressive neural collapse and feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
In deep linear networks, the within-class compression metric decays geometrically and the between-class discrimination metric increases linearly with layer depth.
This pattern of progressive feature compression and discrimination also occurs approximately in deep nonlinear networks.
Increasing the depth of deep linear networks improves generalization performance and feature compression.
Linear layers in hybrid networks mimic the feature learning behavior of deep nonlinear layers.
The theoretical results are validated on synthetic and real datasets.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis assumes nearly orthogonal input data and balanced, low-rank weights, which may not always hold in practice.
The theory is developed for deep linear networks and may not fully capture the behavior of nonlinear networks.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to nonlinear networks.
Investigating the role of depth in other network architectures.
Exploring the implications for transfer learning and architecture design.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, deep learning has proven to be a highly effective tool for learning meaningful features from raw data. However, it remains an open question how deep networks perform hierarchical feature learning across layers. In this work, we attempt to unveil this mystery by investigating the structures of intermediate features. Motivated by our empirical findings that linear layers mimic the roles of deep layers in nonlinear networks for feature learning, we explore how deep linear networks transform input data into output by investigating the output (i.e., features) of each layer after training in the context of multi-class classification problems. Toward this goal, we first define metrics to measure within-class compression and between-class discrimination of intermediate features, respectively. Through theoretical analysis of these two metrics, we show that the evolution of features follows a simple and quantitative pattern from shallow to deep layers when the input data is nearly orthogonal and the network weights are minimum-norm, balanced, and approximate low-rank: Each layer of the linear network progressively compresses within-class features at a geometric rate and discriminates between-class features at a linear rate with respect to the number of layers that data have passed through. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantitative characterization of feature evolution in hierarchical representations of deep linear networks. Empirically, our extensive experiments not only validate our theoretical results numerically but also reveal a similar pattern in deep nonlinear networks which aligns well with recent empirical studies. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical implications of our results in transfer learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Heimine/PNC_DLN.

papers.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
papers.research_question: How can we engineer monosemanticity in toy models? Specifically, can models be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to different minima, and how do bias and number of neurons affect monosemanticity?
papers.core_contribution: Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to minima with moderate negative biases, and increasing the number of neurons per layer increases monosemanticity at the cost of compute.
papers.conclusion: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models is possible via negative biases and wider layers, pointing to future work on robust engineering and understanding polysemantic models.
papers.key_findings:
Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by changing which local minimum training finds.
More monosemantic minima have moderate negative biases, enabling engineering of highly monosemantic models via negative bias initialization and weight decay.
Providing more neurons per layer makes models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost.
In engineered monosemantic models, monosemantic neurons implement a simple algorithm balancing feature recovery against interference, and polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank linear map adjusting confidence.
The conclusions hold for various activation functions and feature frequency distributions.
papers.limitation:
The engineering approach is fragile because it depends on setting a bias weight decay rate that must be slow relative to the rate at which the model learns the task.
Naive introduction of sparsity in model weights results in significant reductions in task performance.
future_direction: Make the bias engineering more robust by tailoring bias decay per neuron or tying it to weight changes, or using regularizers.
Understand the algorithm implemented by highly polysemantic models.
Find ways to reduce compute cost of wider layers without excessive performance degradation.
papers.abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.

papers.title: Layer Collapse Can be Induced by Unstructured Pruning
papers.research_question: When and how can unstructured pruning induce structural effects, specifically layer collapse, in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that unstructured pruning can reduce neuron entropy in rectifier-activated layers, leading to zero-entropy layers that become linearizable and can be removed. It introduces an entropy-guided pruning method (NEPENTHE) that leverages this insight to remove layers with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Unstructured pruning can induce layer collapse in over-parameterized networks, and the proposed entropy-guided method effectively reduces network depth with minimal performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Unstructured pruning naturally reduces the entropy of neurons in rectifier-activated layers.
When a layer's average neuron entropy drops to zero, the layer becomes linearizable and can be removed from the network.
The proposed method NEPENTHE uses an entropy-weighted pruning budget to remove layers with little or no performance degradation.
The layer collapse phenomenon is validated across CNNs, Vision Transformers, and NLP models.
NEPENTHE outperforms baseline pruning methods in reducing network depth while maintaining accuracy.
papers.limitation: For smooth rectifiers (e.g., GELU/SiLU), collapsing layers introduces an approximation error, though it is negligible under the training and pruning regime considered.
future_direction: Combining the approach with structured pruning for further method development.
papers.abstract: Unstructured pruning is a popular compression method for efficiently reducing model parameters. However, while it effectively decreases the number of parameters, it is commonly believed that unstructured pruning cannot shorten the computational critical path, i.e., the maximum number of layers traversed during forward propagation. In this paper, we study when and how unstructured pruning can yield structural effects. For rectifier-activated networks, we introduce the notion of neuron entropy, which quantifies the degree of nonlinearity utilization. We show that magnitude-based pruning naturally lowers this entropy, sometimes down to zero-entropy layers that become linearizable and can thus be removed. Building on this insight, we propose a method that leverages "unstructured" pruning to favor sparsity in low-entropy layers, enabling their complete removal. We validate the phenomenon across CNNs, Vision Transformers, and NLP models: unstructured pruning can induce effective layer removal with little or no performance degradation in over-parameterized networks.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: A Measure of the Complexity of Neural Representations based on Partial Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How is task-relevant information distributed among neurons in a neural network, and how can we quantify the difficulty of accessing information spread across multiple neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces representational complexity, a measure of information sparsity in neural representations derived from partial information decomposition, and shows that it decreases over training and through successive layers in quantized neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Representational complexity is a principled and interpretable summary statistic for analyzing the structure and evolution of neural representations in complex systems.
papers.key_findings:
Representational complexity decreases through successive hidden layers.
Representational complexity decreases over training.
Representational complexity is higher on the test dataset than on the train dataset in later stages of training.
In the case of overfitting (shuffled labels), the gap between train and test representational complexity is wide.
Representational complexity provides a target-oriented measure compared to intrinsic dimensionality.
papers.limitation:
Scaling the approach to larger networks remains a challenge; subsampling suffers from conceptual flaws and coarse-graining bounds become impractically loose for large networks.
The analysis methods are currently limited to quantized networks.
future_direction: Studying overfitting using representational complexity.
Extending the approach to larger networks by computing representational complexity without computing all PID atoms.
papers.abstract: In neural networks, task-relevant information is represented jointly by groups of neurons. However, the specific way in which this mutual information about the classification label is distributed among the individual neurons is not well understood: While parts of it may only be obtainable from specific single neurons, other parts are carried redundantly or synergistically by multiple neurons. We show how Partial Information Decomposition (PID), a recent extension of information theory, can disentangle these different contributions. From this, we introduce the measure of "Representational Complexity", which quantifies the difficulty of accessing information spread across multiple neurons. We show how this complexity is directly computable for smaller layers. For larger layers, we propose subsampling and coarse-graining procedures and prove corresponding bounds on the latter. Empirically, for quantized deep neural networks solving the MNIST and CIFAR10 tasks, we observe that representational complexity decreases both through successive hidden layers and over training, and compare the results to related measures. Overall, we propose representational complexity as a principled and interpretable summary statistic for analyzing the structure and evolution of neural representations and complex systems in general.

papers.title: Complexity for deep neural networks and other characteristics of deep feature representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the nonlinearity and effective dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and how do these measures vary with depth, dataset, and during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two observables—complexity and effective dimension—to quantify the nonlinearity and dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing depth-wise hierarchy, dataset difficulty, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The introduced observables provide quantitative insight into the information processing and feature representations in neural networks, and can be applied to both artificial and biological neural systems, opening up new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Complexity and effective dimension increase with the difficulty of the dataset.
During training, complexity increases first, followed by a rise in effective dimension.
Total correlation between neurons decreases during training, following a power law.
The observables can be applied to biological neural data (mouse visual cortex) and show similar trends.
The observables reveal a depth-wise hierarchy in feature representations, with higher layers having higher complexity and effective dimension for more difficult datasets.
papers.limitation: The method is defined for ReLU activations and may not generalize to other activation functions.
future_direction: Investigate interrelations with the Information Bottleneck principle.
Use methods from statistical physics (e.g., Ising models) for analysis.
Apply the observables to more complex networks and tasks.
papers.abstract: We define a notion of complexity, which quantifies the nonlinearity of the computation of a neural network, as well as a complementary measure of the effective dimension of feature representations. We investigate these observables both for trained networks for various datasets as well as explore their dynamics during training, uncovering in particular power law scaling. These observables can be understood in a dual way as uncovering hidden internal structure of the datasets themselves as a function of scale or depth. The entropic character of the proposed notion of complexity should allow to transfer modes of analysis from neuroscience and statistical physics to the domain of artificial neural networks. The introduced observables can be applied without any change to the analysis of biological neuronal systems.

papers.title: Information Bottleneck: Exact Analysis of (Quantized) Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Are the fitting and compression phases in information bottleneck analysis of neural networks real or artifacts of binning when estimating mutual information?
papers.core_contribution: By using quantized neural networks, mutual information can be computed exactly, showing that fitting and compression phases in IB analysis are not artifacts of binning but depend on network architecture and activation functions.
papers.conclusion: The exact IB analysis confirms that compression phase depends on network architecture, and the proposed framework allows for accurate future studies of IB phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Both fitting and compression phases occur in the output SOFTMAX layer for both TANH and RELU networks.
For hidden layers, fitting occurs for both TANH and RELU, but compression is only observed in the last hidden layer for TANH and not for RELU.
More complex networks with many neurons do not exhibit compression because they are too expressive.
Exact MI computation eliminates measurement artifacts, allowing future research to focus on the utility of IB.
papers.limitation:
The study could not resolve the controversy about the compression phase because it depends on the network architecture.
Studying continuous systems would lead to trivial results, so quantization is used but is not a conceptual limitation.
future_direction: Focus on utility of IB principle for understanding learning dynamics
Accurate future studies of IB phenomena using the proposed framework
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) principle has been suggested as a way to analyze deep neural networks. The learning dynamics are studied by inspecting the mutual information (MI) between the hidden layers and the input and output. Notably, separate fitting and compression phases during training have been reported. This led to some controversy including claims that the observations are not reproducible and strongly dependent on the type of activation function used as well as on the way the MI is estimated. Our study confirms that different ways of binning when computing the MI lead to qualitatively different results, either supporting or refusing IB conjectures. To resolve the controversy, we study the IB principle in settings where MI is non-trivial and can be computed exactly. We monitor the dynamics of quantized neural networks, that is, we discretize the whole deep learning system so that no approximation is required when computing the MI. This allows us to quantify the information flow without measurement errors. In this setting, we observed a fitting phase for all layers and a compression phase for the output layer in all experiments; the compression in the hidden layers was dependent on the type of activation function. Our study shows that the initial IB results were not artifacts of binning when computing the MI. However, the critical claim that the compression phase may not be observed for some networks also holds true.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether reducing monosemantic neurons in neural networks can improve performance, and proposes a method to proactively inhibit them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that reducing monosemantic neurons improves model performance and introduces a metric (Monosemantic Scale) and a method (Reverse Deactivation) to inhibit monosemantic neurons during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that proactively inhibiting monosemantic neurons via the proposed MEmeL method can improve model performance across various tasks and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
MEmeL improves performance on language (GLUE), image (ImageNet), and precipitation forecasting (HKO-7) tasks.
Monosemanticity decreases with model scale, and inhibiting it can lead to better performance.
Naive deactivation methods can intensify monosemanticity, while the proposed Reverse Deactivation method effectively reduces it.
The proposed Monosemantic Scale metric enables efficient online detection of monosemantic neurons.
Pretraining with MEmeL shows greater improvement than finetuning with it, supporting the hypothesis that reducing monosemanticity enhances general ability.
papers.limitation: Extending the research to very large models (e.g., large language models) is appealing yet impossible for research departments due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Extending the method to extremely large models trained on large datasets.
Studying the dynamics of MEmeL in more depth.
papers.abstract: Recently, emergence has received widespread attention from the research community along with the success of large-scale models. Different from the literature, we hypothesize a key factor that promotes the performance during the increase of scale: the reduction of monosemantic neurons that can only form one-to-one correlations with specific features. Monosemantic neurons tend to be sparser and have negative impacts on the performance in large models. Inspired by this insight, we propose an intuitive idea to identify monosemantic neurons and inhibit them. However, achieving this goal is a non-trivial task as there is no unified quantitative evaluation metric and simply banning monosemantic neurons does not promote polysemanticity in neural networks. Therefore, we first propose a new metric to measure the monosemanticity of neurons with the guarantee of efficiency for online computation, then introduce a theoretically supported method to suppress monosemantic neurons and proactively promote the ratios of polysemantic neurons in training neural networks. We validate our conjecture that monosemanticity brings about performance change at different model scales on a variety of neural networks and benchmark datasets in different areas, including language, image, and physics simulation tasks. Further experiments validate our analysis and theory regarding the inhibition of monosemanticity.

papers.title: Entropy and mutual information in models of deep neural networks*
papers.research_question: How can we compute entropies and mutual information in deep neural networks, and what do these quantities reveal about the relationship between compression and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a replica formula to compute entropies and mutual information in stochastic deep neural networks with orthogonally-invariant weights, provides a rigorous proof for two-layer Gaussian networks, and proposes an experimental framework with USV-layers to study compression and generalization.
papers.conclusion: In the proposed setting, the relationship between compression (as measured by mutual information) and generalization remains elusive.
papers.key_findings:
The replica formula provides accurate estimates of entropies and mutual information for large networks, outperforming non-parametric estimators.
For bounded activation functions (e.g., hardtanh), entropies decrease after a certain weight scale, while for unbounded ones (e.g., ReLU) they monotonically increase.
In linear networks trained with USV-layers, mutual information between input and hidden layers increases throughout learning without harming generalization.
In non-linear networks on correlated data, the expected compression-generalization relationship (information bottleneck) is not clearly observed.
The proposed USV-layers allow the replica formula to remain valid during learning, enabling the study of information-theoretic quantities.
papers.limitation:
The assumption of orthogonally-invariant weight matrices is restrictive and may not hold in general.
The addition of small Gaussian noise to compute mutual information is arbitrary and may affect the results.
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine a class of stochastic deep learning models with a tractable method to compute information-theoretic quantities. Our contributions are three-fold: (i) we show how entropies and mutual informations can be derived from heuristic statistical physics methods, under the assumption that weight matrices are independent and orthogonally-invariant. (ii) We extend particular cases in which this result is known to be rigorously exact by providing a proof for two-layers networks with Gaussian random weights, using the recently introduced adaptive interpolation method. (iii) We propose an experiment framework with generative models of synthetic datasets, on which we train deep neural networks with a weight constraint designed so that the assumption in (i) is verified during learning. We study the behavior of entropies and mutual informations throughout learning and conclude that, in the proposed setting, the relationship between compression and generalization remains elusive.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Deep Neural Networks by Leveraging Adversarial Examples
papers.research_question: What do neurons in deep neural networks truly detect, and are deep visual representations robust distributed codes of visual concepts? The paper investigates these questions using adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neurons in DNNs are not true object detectors but respond to discriminative patches, and deep visual representations are not robust. It then proposes an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss to improve interpretability and consistency of representations.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves the interpretability and robustness of DNNs, allowing human users to understand model predictions and errors through interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts but respond to objects/parts as recurrent discriminative patches.
Deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because representations of adversarial images are inconsistent with those of real images.
Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves interpretability, making neurons detect true objects/parts and representations more consistent.
Interpretable representations enable tracing predictions back to influential neurons, explaining how models make predictions and errors.
Adversarial training also improves model robustness against adversarial attacks.
papers.limitation: Adversarial training causes a drop in accuracy on real images, representing a trade-off between performance and interpretability/robustness.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance on a wide array of tasks, but they are usually considered opaque since internal structure and learned parameters are not interpretable. In this paper, we re-examine the internal representations of DNNs using adversarial images, which are generated by an ensemble-optimization algorithm. We find that: (1) the neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts, but respond to objects/parts only as recurrent discriminative patches; (2) deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because the representations of adversarial images are largely not consistent with those of real images, although they have similar visual appearance, both of which are different from previous findings. To further improve the interpretability of DNNs, we propose an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss such that the neurons are endowed with human-interpretable concepts. The induced interpretable representations enable us to trace eventual outcomes back to influential neurons. Therefore, human users can know how the models make predictions, as well as when and why they make errors.

papers.title: Estimating Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we accurately estimate the mutual information between the input and internal representations of a deep neural network, and what geometric phenomenon (clustering) underlies the observed compression of mutual information during training?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a rigorous framework for accurate estimation of mutual information in noisy DNNs and identifies geometric clustering of internal representations as the driver of compression, clarifying that binning-based measures in prior work track clustering rather than mutual information.
papers.conclusion: Clustering of internal representations is the fundamental geometric phenomenon of interest, which occurs in both deterministic and noisy networks; mutual information is only meaningful in the presence of noise and tracks the same clustering effect, while binning-based measures are simple proxies for clustering.
papers.key_findings:
In deterministic DNNs, mutual information I(X; Tℓ) is vacuous (infinite or constant), so the compression observed via binning in prior works actually measures clustering of representations.
In noisy DNNs, compression of I(X; Tℓ) during training is driven by progressive geometric clustering of representations from the same class.
Clustering of internal representations occurs in both deterministic and noisy DNNs, and can be measured by the discrete entropy H(Bin(Tℓ)).
The relationship between compression (or clustering) and generalization performance is not straightforward and may not be causal.
The proposed Sample Propagation estimator provides a theoretically grounded method for estimating mutual information in noisy DNNs.
papers.limitation:
Mutual information estimation is statistically difficult and requires a number of samples that can be exponential in the dimension of the hidden layer.
The binning-based measure H(Bin(Tℓ)) is not an accurate estimator of mutual information and its interpretation depends on the bin size.
future_direction: Develop efficient methods to track clustering in high-dimensional spaces.
Investigate the connection between clustering and generalization theoretically and experimentally.
Develop a new regularization procedure for DNN training that encourages intermediate layers to increase a clustering-based analog of I(Y; Tℓ).
papers.abstract: We study the flow of information and the evolution of internal representations during deep neural network (DNN) training, aiming to demystify the compression aspect of the information bottleneck theory. The theory suggests that DNN training comprises a rapid fitting phase followed by a slower compression phase, in which the mutual information $I(X;T)$ between the input $X$ and internal representations $T$ decreases. Several papers observe compression of estimated mutual information on different DNN models, but the true $I(X;T)$ over these networks is provably either constant (discrete $X$) or infinite (continuous $X$). This work explains the discrepancy between theory and experiments, and clarifies what was actually measured by these past works. To this end, we introduce an auxiliary (noisy) DNN framework for which $I(X;T)$ is a meaningful quantity that depends on the network's parameters. This noisy framework is shown to be a good proxy for the original (deterministic) DNN both in terms of performance and the learned representations. We then develop a rigorous estimator for $I(X;T)$ in noisy DNNs and observe compression in various models. By relating $I(X;T)$ in the noisy DNN to an information-theoretic communication problem, we show that compression is driven by the progressive clustering of hidden representations of inputs from the same class. Several methods to directly monitor clustering of hidden representations, both in noisy and deterministic DNNs, are used to show that meaningful clusters form in the $T$ space. Finally, we return to the estimator of $I(X;T)$ employed in past works, and demonstrate that while it fails to capture the true (vacuous) mutual information, it does serve as a measure for clustering. This clarifies the past observations of compression and isolates the geometric clustering of hidden representations as the true phenomenon of interest.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: Task complexity shapes internal representations and robustness in neural networks
papers.research_question: How does task complexity influence the internal representations and robustness of neural networks? The paper introduces probes to quantify how task difficulty shapes the topology and robustness of learned representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a suite of data-agnostic probes to quantify how task complexity shapes internal representations and robustness in neural networks. It finds that weight signs and bipartite topology are crucial for performance, especially in hard tasks, and suggests implications for model compression.
papers.conclusion: Our study highlights the impact of task complexity on learned representations, emphasizing the crucial role of weight signs and connectivity. Practically, layers where weight signs dominate performance could be candidates for binarization during inference.
papers.key_findings:
Binarizing an MLP trained on a hard task causes accuracy to collapse to chance, while an easy-task model remains robust.
Pruning low-magnitude edges in binarized hard-task models reveals a sharp phase transition in performance.
Moderate noise injection can boost accuracy via a stochastic-resonance effect linked to optimal sign flips of small-magnitude weights.
Preserving only the sign structure through bipartite network randomizations suffices to maintain high accuracy, indicating the importance of signs over precise magnitudes.
In DistilBERT, early layers are less robust to binarization and pruning than later layers, which can be binarized without loss.
future_direction: Explore the link between probe-based robustness measures and representational similarity metrics (e.g., CKA, RSA).
papers.abstract: Neural networks excel across a wide range of tasks, yet remain black boxes. In particular, how their internal representations are shaped by the complexity of the input data and the problems they solve remains obscure. In this work, we introduce a suite of five data-agnostic probes-pruning, binarization, noise injection, sign flipping, and bipartite network randomization-to quantify how task difficulty influences the topology and robustness of representations in multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). MLPs are represented as signed, weighted bipartite graphs from a network science perspective. We contrast easy and hard classification tasks on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. We show that binarizing weights in hard-task models collapses accuracy to chance, whereas easy-task models remain robust. We also find that pruning low-magnitude edges in binarized hard-task models reveals a sharp phase-transition in performance. Moreover, moderate noise injection can enhance accuracy, resembling a stochastic-resonance effect linked to optimal sign flips of small-magnitude weights. Finally, preserving only the sign structure-instead of precise weight magnitudes-through bipartite network randomizations suffices to maintain high accuracy. These phenomena define a model- and modality-agnostic measure of task complexity: the performance gap between full-precision and binarized or shuffled neural network performance. Our findings highlight the crucial role of signed bipartite topology in learned representations and suggest practical strategies for model compression and interpretability that align with task complexity.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
papers.research_question: Do current theories of feature learning measure the quality of learned features (which impacts generalization) or just the strength of representation changes?
papers.core_contribution: Current feature learning theories measure the strength of representation changes (FL strength) but not the quality of features, and these are decoupled. The paper introduces the FL gap to measure feature quality and shows that FL strength does not predict generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current theories of feature learning do not predict generalization because they measure strength rather than quality, indicating the need for a more comprehensive FL theory.
papers.key_findings:
The feature learning gap (∆NT) quantifies the performance improvement of neural networks over kernel methods.
Current FL definitions (NTK-based, CK-based, superposition-based) measure FL strength, not feature quality.
FL strength metrics (e.g., SNT, SCK) fail to distinguish between networks trained on true vs. shuffled labels, indicating decoupling from generalization.
The NTK-based FL strength can be manipulated by output scaling without affecting generalization.
CK-based cumulative utility does not differentiate between shuffled and non-shuffled data.
future_direction: Developing a more comprehensive feature learning theory that links feature learning to generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks outperform kernel methods, sometimes by orders of magnitude, e.g. on staircase functions. This advantage stems from the ability of neural networks to learn features, adapting their hidden representations to better capture the data. We introduce a concept we call feature quality to measure this performance improvement. We examine existing theories of feature learning and demonstrate empirically that they primarily assess the strength of feature learning, rather than the quality of the learned features themselves. Consequently, current theories of feature learning do not provide a sufficient foundation for developing theories of neural network generalization.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Uncovering Layer-Dependent Activation Sparsity Patterns in ReLU Transformers
papers.research_question: How does token-level sparsity evolve over training in ReLU Transformers, and how do sparsity patterns differ across layers and between token, sequence, and batch levels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparsity patterns in ReLU Transformers are layer-dependent, with the first and last layers exhibiting inverted sparsity behaviors, and that neuron death is driven by training dynamics rather than random outliers.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity in ReLU Transformers varies systematically across layers, with the first and last layers being inverses in sparsity behavior, and that one can prune a significant fraction of hidden units without affecting accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Different layers in a ReLU Transformer exhibit distinct sparsity patterns, with the first layer using few hidden units per batch but using them frequently, and the last layer using many hidden units per batch but infrequently per token.
Sparsity patterns at token, sequence, and batch levels often anticorrelate, with layers that use few hidden units per token using many over a batch.
Neuron death (hidden units that never activate) is driven by training dynamics and occurs in specific regimes, rather than randomly.
A significant fraction of hidden units (about 5%) are never used from initialization, suggesting potential for better initialization methods.
Pruning hidden units that are never used after a point in training does not harm model performance, indicating potential for compute savings.
papers.limitation: The study focuses exclusively on small models and ReLU activation functions, which limits immediate applicability to modern foundation models.
future_direction: Investigate changes to initialization functions or model structure to allow more effective use of capacity in both ReLU and more competitive activation functions.
Study the underlying similarities in features learned between ReLU and smoothly-activated networks.
papers.abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that MLPs within ReLU Transformers exhibit high levels of sparsity, with many of their activations equal to zero for any given token. We build on that work to more deeply explore how token-level sparsity evolves over the course of training, and how it connects to broader sparsity patterns over the course of a sequence or batch, demonstrating that the different layers within small transformers exhibit distinctly layer-specific patterns on both of these fronts. In particular, we demonstrate that the first and last layer of the network have distinctive and in many ways inverted relationships to sparsity, and explore implications for the structure of feature representations being learned at different depths of the model. We additionally explore the phenomenon of ReLU dimensions "turning off", and show evidence suggesting that "neuron death" is being primarily driven by the dynamics of training, rather than simply occurring randomly or accidentally as a result of outliers.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: From Tokens to Thoughts: How LLMs and Humans Trade Compression for Meaning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how LLMs and humans balance compression and meaning in conceptual representation, specifically examining the alignment of LLM-emergent categories with human-defined categories, the fidelity to fine-grained semantic structure like typicality, and the differences in compression-meaning trade-off strategies.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs and humans employ different strategies in the compression-meaning trade-off: LLMs achieve broad categorical alignment but optimize for aggressive statistical compression at the cost of semantic nuance, while humans maintain 'inefficient' representations that preserve rich contextual structure. Encoder models surprisingly outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs and humans optimize differently for compression versus meaning preservation, with LLMs favoring statistical efficiency and humans favoring adaptive utility. This divergence highlights the need for AI models that preserve conceptual 'inefficiencies' essential for human-like understanding.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs capture broad categorical boundaries aligned with human categories but show weak correlation with fine-grained typicality judgments.
LLMs achieve more optimal information-theoretic compression (lower L objective) than human conceptual structures.
Encoder models (e.g., BERT) match or exceed the human-alignment performance of decoder models 100x larger, indicating distinct representational mechanisms for understanding vs. generation.
Training dynamics analysis of OLMo-7B reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization where semantic processing migrates to mid-network layers.
Human categories appear less statistically efficient but are optimized for adaptive flexibility and rich semantic preservation, unlike LLMs which prioritize compression.
papers.limitation:
The metrics used capture information-compression trade-off and geometric efficiency but do not directly measure all aspects of human-style conceptual abstraction or reasoning.
The analysis is limited to open-source models, excluding closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5 and Claude.
future_direction: Incorporate hierarchical and compositional structure to capture nested relationships between categories.
Incorporate feature- and relation-based biases to help models focus on meaningful perceptual or functional attributes.
Incorporate theory- or causally grounded priors to constrain learning and support flexible generalization.
papers.abstract: Humans organize knowledge into compact conceptual categories that balance compression with semantic richness. Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive linguistic abilities, but whether they navigate this same compression-meaning trade-off remains unclear. We apply an Information Bottleneck framework to compare human conceptual structure with embeddings from 40+ LLMs using classic categorization benchmarks. We find that LLMs broadly align with human category boundaries, yet fall short on fine-grained semantic distinctions. Unlike humans, who maintain ``inefficient'' representations that preserve contextual nuance, LLMs aggressively compress, achieving more optimal information-theoretic compression at the cost of semantic richness. Surprisingly, encoder models outperform much larger decoder models in human alignment, suggesting that understanding and generation rely on distinct representational mechanisms. Training-dynamics analysis reveals a two-phase trajectory: rapid initial concept formation followed by architectural reorganization, during which semantic processing migrates from deep to mid-network layers as the model discovers increasingly efficient, sparser encodings. These divergent strategies, where LLMs optimize for compression and humans for adaptive utility, reveal fundamental differences between artificial and natural intelligence. This highlights the need for models that preserve the conceptual ``inefficiencies'' essential for human-like understanding.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task.
