To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Information Bottleneck Analysis of Deep Neural Networks via Lossy Compression
papers.research_question: How can we perform Information Bottleneck analysis on general neural networks by overcoming the curse of dimensionality in mutual information estimation via lossy compression?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for Information Bottleneck analysis of general neural networks by using lossy compression to overcome the curse of dimensionality in mutual information estimation, enabling analysis of larger networks and revealing multiple compression/fitting phases during training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables Information Bottleneck analysis for larger neural networks by mitigating the curse of dimensionality through lossy compression, revealing new features in mutual information dynamics during training.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed compression-based mutual information estimator performs accurately on synthetic datasets with known mutual information.
Information plane analysis of a convolutional classifier on MNIST reveals multiple compression and fitting phases during training, which correspond to different learning regimes (accelerated, stationary, or decelerated loss drop).
The weighted Kozachenko-Leonenko entropy estimator, when combined with compression, outperforms other tested estimators and MINE on high-dimensional synthetic data.
Theoretical bounds are provided for mutual information estimation under lossy compression, showing that the method can track the true mutual information within the errors of the estimator and the compression bounds.
The method relies on the manifold hypothesis and uses autoencoders for compression, which can be applied to stochastic neural networks to estimate information flow.
papers.limitation: The method relies on the manifold hypothesis and may lose information during compression, as arbitrary amounts of information can be lost if the compression is not lossless.
future_direction: Using normalizing flows for lossless and information-preserving compression to improve the approach.
Applying the method to various large neural networks and performing corresponding information plane analysis.
papers.abstract: The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle offers an information-theoretic framework for analyzing the training process of deep neural networks (DNNs). Its essence lies in tracking the dynamics of two mutual information (MI) values: between the hidden layer output and the DNN input/target. According to the hypothesis put forth by Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby (2017), the training process consists of two distinct phases: fitting and compression. The latter phase is believed to account for the good generalization performance exhibited by DNNs. Due to the challenging nature of estimating MI between high-dimensional random vectors, this hypothesis was only partially verified for NNs of tiny sizes or specific types, such as quantized NNs. In this paper, we introduce a framework for conducting IB analysis of general NNs. Our approach leverages the stochastic NN method proposed by Goldfeld et al. (2019) and incorporates a compression step to overcome the obstacles associated with high dimensionality. In other words, we estimate the MI between the compressed representations of high-dimensional random vectors. The proposed method is supported by both theoretical and practical justifications. Notably, we demonstrate the accuracy of our estimator through synthetic experiments featuring predefined MI values and comparison with MINE (Belghazi et al., 2018). Finally, we perform IB analysis on a close-to-real-scale convolutional DNN, which reveals new features of the MI dynamics.

papers.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does binarising sparse autoencoder activations improve the interpretability and monosemanticity of the discovered features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces binary sparse autoencoders and transcoders, finding that binarisation improves unweighted feature interpretability but increases reconstruction error and ultra-high frequency features, suggesting polysemanticity may be an ineliminable property of neural activations.
papers.conclusion: Binary sparse coders are not recommended for most purposes; the attempt to eliminate polysemanticity by binarising activations merely shifted it to high-frequency features, supporting the idea that polysemanticity is ineliminable.
papers.key_findings:
Binarisation improves unweighted average feature interpretability but increases the cross-entropy loss when patched into the base model.
Binarisation does not increase interpretability when features are weighted by their firing frequencies.
Binary transcoders have more ultra-high frequency features than continuous ones, and these tend to have low interpretability scores.
Binary sparse coders underperform continuous ones in sparse probing evaluation before fine-tuning, but after fine-tuning they outperform.
There is little relationship between interpretability and causal importance of features except at the extremes of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single dataset (SmolLM2 training corpus) may limit applicability.
Some sparse coders exhibited high numbers of dead neurons.
Results may change at higher sparse coder widths.
future_direction: Exploring mixed architectures with a mixture of binary and continuous features.
Dynamically determining the appropriate mixture of binary and continuous features in a data-dependent way.
Further investigation of the promising performance of binary sparse coders on sparse probing tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to decompose neural network activations into sparsely activating features, but many SAE features are only interpretable at high activation strengths. To address this issue we propose to use binary sparse autoencoders (BAEs) and binary transcoders (BTCs), which constrain all activations to be zero or one. We find that binarisation significantly improves the interpretability and monosemanticity of the discovered features, while increasing reconstruction error. By eliminating the distinction between high and low activation strengths, we prevent uninterpretable information from being smuggled in through the continuous variation in feature activations. However, we also find that binarisation increases the number of uninterpretable ultra-high frequency features, and when interpretability scores are frequency-adjusted, the scores for continuous sparse coders are slightly better than those of binary ones. This suggests that polysemanticity may be an ineliminable property of neural activations.

papers.title: Pruning Redundant Mappings in Transformer Models via Spectral-Normalized Identity Prior
papers.research_question: Can structured pruning be performed on Transformer models by penalizing residual modules toward identity mappings, and how can spectral normalization improve pruning effectiveness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNIP, a structured pruning method that uses spectral normalization and identity prior to prune Transformer modules (attention heads and FFN layers) effectively while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a structured pruning method (SNIP) for compressing Transformer models, achieving effective pruning on BERT while maintaining performance, and shows the importance of the Lipschitz condition for pruning.
papers.key_findings:
SNIP achieves effective pruning (up to 50% compression) while maintaining comparable performance on GLUE tasks.
Spectral normalization stabilizes the distribution of post-activation values and improves pruning effectiveness.
Different tasks lead to similar but not identical pruning patterns for attention heads.
FFN layers are more critical than attention layers for some tasks (pruning FFN damages performance more).
Separate pruning of attention and FFN layers is more flexible and effective than pruning whole layers.
future_direction: Reduce the width of Transformer layers (hidden dimension) for higher compression
Jointly use the proposed approach with other compression methods
papers.abstract: Traditional (unstructured) pruning methods for a Transformer model focus on regularizing the individual weights by penalizing them toward zero. In this work, we explore spectralnormalized identity priors (SNIP), a structured pruning approach that penalizes an entire residual module in a Transformer model toward an identity mapping. Our method identifies and discards unimportant non-linear mappings in the residual connections by applying a thresholding operator on the function norm. It is applicable to any structured module, including a single attention head, an entire attention block, or a feed-forward subnetwork. Furthermore, we introduce spectral normalization to stabilize the distribution of the post-activation values of the Transformer layers, further improving the pruning effectiveness of the proposed methodology. We conduct experiments with BERT on 5 GLUE benchmark tasks to demonstrate that SNIP achieves effective pruning results while maintaining comparable performance. Specifically, we improve the performance over the state-of-the-art by 0.5 to 1.0% on average at 50% compression ratio.

papers.title: Selectivity considered harmful: evaluating the causal impact of class selectivity in DNNs
papers.research_question: Is class selectivity in individual units necessary and/or sufficient for DNN function?
papers.core_contribution: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can even impair it; reducing selectivity can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can be detrimental. This encourages caution when focusing on single-unit properties and emphasizes distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
Reducing class selectivity can improve test accuracy, e.g., by over 2% for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet.
Class selectivity can be reduced by a factor of 2.5 in ResNet20 on CIFAR10 with no impact on test accuracy, and nearly to zero with only a small drop.
Increasing class selectivity significantly decreases test accuracy across all models and datasets.
The regularizer suppresses selectivity generally, not just by rotating it off-axis, indicating viability of low-selectivity distributed representations.
Networks are at a performance cliff with regard to class selectivity; naturally learned levels are at the limit of what impairs performance.
papers.abstract: The properties of individual neurons are often analyzed in order to understand the biological and artificial neural networks in which they're embedded. Class selectivity-typically defined as how different a neuron's responses are across different classes of stimuli or data samples-is commonly used for this purpose. However, it remains an open question whether it is necessary and/or sufficient for deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn class selectivity in individual units. We investigated the causal impact of class selectivity on network function by directly regularizing for or against class selectivity. Using this regularizer to reduce class selectivity across units in convolutional neural networks increased test accuracy by over 2% for ResNet18 trained on Tiny ImageNet. For ResNet20 trained on CIFAR10 we could reduce class selectivity by a factor of 2.5 with no impact on test accuracy, and reduce it nearly to zero with only a small ($\sim$2%) drop in test accuracy. In contrast, regularizing to increase class selectivity significantly decreased test accuracy across all models and datasets. These results indicate that class selectivity in individual units is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary, and can even impair DNN performance. They also encourage caution when focusing on the properties of single units as representative of the mechanisms by which DNNs function.

papers.title: Interpreting Convolutional Neural Networks Through Compression
papers.research_question: How can compression, specifically filter pruning, be used to interpret convolutional neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compression via filter pruning, using the CAR importance index, can make CNNs more interpretable by removing redundant filters and enabling class-based filter interpretation.
papers.conclusion: Structural compression (filter pruning) of CNNs has the dual purposes of saving memory and computational cost and making the networks more humanly interpretable, and the CAR method effectively prunes redundant filters and provides class-based interpretations.
papers.key_findings:
The CAR compression algorithm prunes filters with visually redundant pattern selectivity, such as color-selective filters, indicating shape is more important for object recognition.
Out of the top 20 CAR-pruned filters in AlexNet, 17 in the first layer and 14 in the second layer are color-selective filters.
The class-based CAR index (CAR c) provides a meaningful interpretation of each filter that is consistent with the visualized pattern selectivity of that filter.
The CAR algorithm achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy and compression rate compared to other structural compression schemes.
The algorithm tends to keep at least one filter from each group of visually similar filters, indicating it identifies redundant filters.
future_direction: Applying the importance index to compare any two networks, particularly various CNNs with different structures.
Adapting the CAR structural compression algorithm and interpretations to fully-connected networks.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieve state-of-the-art performance in a wide variety of tasks in computer vision. However, interpreting CNNs still remains a challenge. This is mainly due to the large number of parameters in these networks. Here, we investigate the role of compression and particularly pruning filters in the interpretation of CNNs. We exploit our recently-proposed greedy structural compression scheme that prunes filters in a trained CNN. In our compression, the filter importance index is defined as the classification accuracy reduction (CAR) of the network after pruning that filter. The filters are then iteratively pruned based on the CAR index. We demonstrate the interpretability of CAR-compressed CNNs by showing that our algorithm prunes filters with visually redundant pattern selectivity. Specifically, we show the importance of shape-selective filters for object recognition, as opposed to color-selective filters. Out of top 20 CAR-pruned filters in AlexNet, 17 of them in the first layer and 14 of them in the second layer are color-selective filters. Finally, we introduce a variant of our CAR importance index that quantifies the importance of each image class to each CNN filter. We show that the most and the least important class labels present a meaningful interpretation of each filter that is consistent with the visualized pattern selectivity of that filter.

papers.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to formulate a statistical model for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations, and design an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a statistical framework for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations and proposes Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and improved empirical performance.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a statistical framework and the GBA algorithm for provable feature recovery in SAEs, advancing mechanistic interpretability with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a statistical model that formalizes polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts.
Introduces Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm that uses bias adaptation to control neuron sparsity without hyperparameter tuning.
Provides the first provable recovery guarantee for an SAE algorithm, showing GBA recovers all monosemantic features under the statistical model.
Empirically demonstrates GBA achieves superior sparsity-loss trade-off and feature consistency on LLMs up to 1.5B parameters compared to baseline methods.
future_direction: Extending the statistical framework to more complex data distributions.
Scaling GBA to larger models.
Exploring applications in model steering and control.
papers.abstract: We study the challenge of achieving theoretically grounded feature recovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for the interpretation of Large Language Models. Existing SAE training algorithms often lack rigorous mathematical guarantees and suffer from practical limitations such as hyperparameter sensitivity and instability. To address these issues, we first propose a novel statistical framework for the feature recovery problem, which includes a new notion of feature identifiability by modeling polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts. Building on this framework, we introduce a new SAE training algorithm based on ``bias adaptation'', a technique that adaptively adjusts neural network bias parameters to ensure appropriate activation sparsity. We theoretically \highlight{prove that this algorithm correctly recovers all monosemantic features} when input data is sampled from our proposed statistical model. Furthermore, we develop an improved empirical variant, Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), and \highlight{demonstrate its superior performance against benchmark methods when applied to LLMs with up to 1.5 billion parameters}. This work represents a foundational step in demystifying SAE training by providing the first SAE algorithm with theoretical recovery guarantees, thereby advancing the development of more transparent and trustworthy AI systems through enhanced mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Interpretation of Deep CNN Based on Learning Feature Reconstruction With Feedback Weights
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a deep CNN by learning feature reconstruction with feedback weights to understand which features contribute to recognition and evaluate recognition success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN to interpret the deep CNN by reconstructing features and analyzing clusters in feature spaces, enabling accurate recovery of ground truth, generation of novel inputs, and identification of recognition errors.
papers.conclusion: The feedback weights provide a means to interpret the deep CNN, and the clustering-based interpretation and feature interpolation algorithm offer meaningful insights into neuron collaboration and recognition.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach accurately recovers ground truth input under data corruption.
It generates novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations.
It identifies incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of error in feature spaces.
The experiments on ModelNet datasets show higher accuracy than conventional approaches.
future_direction: Extend interpretation to connect semantic knowledge while extracting meaningful features using a deep neural network.
papers.abstract: Interpreting a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) involves identifying the features in a hierarchy of layers that contribute to recognition. Although the current approaches serve as methods to interpret a deep CNN, further advancement is required for a more accurate and efficient way of understanding how a hierarchy of features formed by a deep CNN contributes to recognition. In this paper, we propose attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN as a means of learning how recognition is performed by the feedforward CNN. In other words, the features reconstructed in a hierarchy of the feedback CNN represent those learned by the feedforward CNN. By analyzing how clusters are formed in the layers of feature spaces in the feedback CNN, we can interpret which features critically contribute to recognition. It also helps to evaluate whether or not recognition is done successfully. In order to show this, we experimentally verify the capabilities of the proposed approach in terms of 1) accurately recovering the ground truth input under data corruption; 2) generating novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations; and 3) identifying incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of the error in feature spaces. The experiments conducted on the ModelNet datasets indicate that the proposed approach offers an extended capability of interpreting a deep CNN as described above with higher accuracy than the conventional approaches.

papers.title: Quality of internal representation shapes learning performance in feedback neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the interplay between internal network dynamics and target properties shape learning performance in feedback neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Learning performance in feedback networks is maximized when the target frequency matches a resonance frequency determined by internal connectivity, corresponding to high-dimensional and desynchronized internal representations.
papers.conclusion: The quality of internal representation, shaped by the interplay between network connectivity and target dynamics, is a major determinant of learning success in feedback networks.
papers.key_findings:
Learning performance in feedback networks is non-monotonic with target frequency, with an optimal frequency that decreases with increasing connectivity strength.
The optimal frequency corresponds to a resonance where the internal representation has maximal dimensionality and minimal synchrony.
The condition number of the cross-correlation matrix is minimized at the resonance frequency, making learning more robust.
These findings hold across different training algorithms (LS, ridge, RLS) and for both linear and non-linear networks.
In non-linear networks, the resonance frequency increases with target amplitude.
papers.abstract: The authors find a resonance frequency at which feedback neural networks reproduce a sinusoidal wave, and show that network performance is determined by the robustness of the corresponding internal representation.

papers.title: Learning-induced reorganization of number neurons and emergence of numerical representations in a biologically inspired neural network
papers.research_question: How does numerosity training reorganize neuronal tuning properties and population-level representations in a biologically inspired neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Numerosity training reorganizes neuronal tuning and population representations, leading to the emergence of sharp numerosity tuning and latent magnitude representations in a biologically inspired neural network.
papers.conclusion: Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.
papers.key_findings:
Numerosity training reorganizes spontaneous number neurons (SPONs), with most SPONs dropping or switching their preferred numerosity.
Training increases tuning precision, stability, and selectivity of number-sensitive neurons, especially in the IPS layer.
Ablation shows that persistent SPONs are not critical for numerosity classification; newly trained and switched neurons are more important.
Representational similarity analysis reveals increased differentiation between numerosities after training.
Multidimensional scaling reveals latent representations of absolute magnitude and relative magnitude (midpoint anchoring) post-training.
papers.abstract: Number sense, the ability to decipher quantity, forms the foundation for mathematical cognition. How number sense emerges with learning is, however, not known. Here we use a biologically-inspired neural architecture comprising cortical layers V1, V2, V3, and intraparietal sulcus (IPS) to investigate how neural representations change with numerosity training. Learning dramatically reorganized neuronal tuning properties at both the single unit and population levels, resulting in the emergence of sharply-tuned representations of numerosity in the IPS layer. Ablation analysis revealed that spontaneous number neurons observed prior to learning were not critical to formation of number representations post-learning. Crucially, multidimensional scaling of population responses revealed the emergence of absolute and relative magnitude representations of quantity, including mid-point anchoring. These learnt representations may underlie changes from logarithmic to cyclic and linear mental number lines that are characteristic of number sense development in humans. Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.

papers.title: How Does a Transformer Learn Compression? An Attention Study on Huffman and LZ4
papers.research_question: Can Transformers learn compression algorithms like Huffman and LZ4, and do their attention mechanisms provide interpretable insights into how they internalize these algorithms as finite state machines?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn compression algorithms, and their attention maps reveal how the encoder captures input statistics (state) and the decoder generates output bits, providing interpretability and evidence of their ability to understand finite state machines.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn compression algorithms, and their attention mechanisms provide interpretable insights into how they capture input state and generate output, suggesting their potential for understanding finite state machines.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy in learning Huffman and LZ4 compression algorithms.
Attention maps show the encoder's self-attention captures input context (e.g., previous symbols in Markov sources), forming a state.
Cross-attention maps clearly show the association between input symbols and output bits, indicating the decoder uses the encoder's state.
Ablation studies show that models without self-attention perform worse, highlighting its role in learning context.
For LZ4, attention maps show block-like patterns, indicating the model learns to associate input and output units.
papers.limitation: The encoder-only Transformer struggles with longer sequences for conditional Huffman encoding, potentially requiring larger models and more data.
papers.abstract: Transformers have excelled in natural language processing and vision domains. This leads to the intriguing proposition: can Transformers be adapted to a more generalized framework, such as understanding general finite state machines? To explore this, we trained a Transformer network on compression algorithms like Huffman and LZ4, viewing them as stepping stones towards mastering general finite state machines. Our analysis indicates that Transformers can adeptly internalize these methods and replicate essential states, echoing human-like interpretation via their attention mechanisms. This provides evidence of their capability to decipher practical finite state machines. Examining the attention maps offers insights into the Transformer’s methodology when engaging with these compression techniques. In Huffman encodings, the encoder predominantly focuses on input statistics to define the present state, which the decoder subsequently leverages to produce output bits. Remarkably, with a 2nd-order Markov input, the encoder’s attention is prominently directed at the previous two symbols, underscoring its proficiency in summarizing input statistics. The cross-attention maps further elucidate the exact association between input symbols and output bits. For the more complex LZ4 compression, the attention maps vividly portray the Transformer’s processing of input sequences and the close linkage between the input and resulting output bit stream. This study underscores the Transformer’s proficiency in comprehending compression algorithms and its keen ability to grasp input statistics, implying that its mechanisms, as illustrated by attention maps, provide profound interpretability.

papers.title: Robustness to Transformations Across Categories: Is Robustness To Transformations Driven by Invariant Neural Representations?
papers.research_question: To what extent do invariant neural representations drive robustness to transformations in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), and under what conditions do such invariant representations emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Invariant neural representations do not always drive robustness to transformations; they only emerge as the number of transformed categories in the training set increases, and this phenomenon is more prominent for local transformations (e.g., blur) than for geometric ones (e.g., rotation).
papers.conclusion: Invariant neural representations emerge at the individual neuron level and drive robustness to transformations for categories not seen transformed during training, but only when a sufficient number of categories are seen transformed.
papers.key_findings:
Networks show robustness to transformations for categories seen transformed during training even in the absence of invariant neural representations.
Invariant neural representations emerge as the number of transformed categories in the training set is increased.
The increase in invariance and across-category robustness is much more prominent for local transformations (e.g., blur, high-pass filtering) than for geometric transformations (e.g., rotation, thinning).
Invariance emerges at the individual neural level and is nearly identical for seen- and unseen-transformed categories when the number of seen-transformed categories is large.
Across-category robustness is correlated with the amount of invariance, while within-category robustness can be achieved without invariance.
papers.limitation:
The study examines how networks attain invariance for individual types of transformations independently, whereas multiple types of transformations often co-occur in real-world scenarios.
It does not explore how individual neurons respond to transformations that fall outside the range of the training transformations.
future_direction: Understanding why invariant representations emerge for some transformations and what are the neural mechanisms for robustness when there is a lack of invariance.
Exploring how individual neurons develop invariance in the presence of multiple transformation types.
Investigating how individual neurons respond to transformations outside the training regime.
papers.abstract: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have demonstrated impressive robustness to recognize objects under transformations (eg. blur or noise) when these transformations are included in the training set. A hypothesis to explain such robustness is that DCNNs develop invariant neural representations that remain unaltered when the image is transformed. However, to what extent this hypothesis holds true is an outstanding question, as robustness to transformations could be achieved with properties different from invariance, eg. parts of the network could be specialized to recognize either transformed or non-transformed images. This paper investigates the conditions under which invariant neural representations emerge by leveraging that they facilitate robustness to transformations beyond the training distribution. Concretely, we analyze a training paradigm in which only some object categories are seen transformed during training and evaluate whether the DCNN is robust to transformations across categories not seen transformed. Our results with state-of-the-art DCNNs indicate that invariant neural representations do not always drive robustness to transformations, as networks show robustness for categories seen transformed during training even in the absence of invariant neural representations. Invariance only emerges as the number of transformed categories in the training set is increased. This phenomenon is much more prominent with local transformations such as blurring and high-pass filtering than geometric transformations such as rotation and thinning, which entail changes in the spatial arrangement of the object. Our results contribute to a better understanding of invariant neural representations in deep learning and the conditions under which it spontaneously emerges.

papers.title: Adversarial Perturbations Are Not So Weird: Entanglement of Robust and Non-Robust Features in Neural Network Classifiers
papers.research_question: What is the nature of the non-robust features responsible for adversarial vulnerability in neural network classifiers, and how are they related to robust features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that non-robust features in standard neural network classifiers are entangled with robust, human-interpretable features, and that this entanglement explains adversarial vulnerability. It also shows that robust classifiers are more effective sources for generating transferable adversarial examples.
papers.conclusion: Non-robust features in neural network classifiers are often entangled with robust features, meaning adversarial perturbations exploit patterns that are components of human-interpretable features, making them less 'weird' than previously thought.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-robust and negative-robust classifiers achieve above-chance accuracy on robustified test sets, indicating that non-robust features are entangled with robust features (Type B features).
Robust features are more universal than non-robust features, as evidenced by standard classifiers performing well on test sets robustified with respect to robust classifiers.
Adversarial examples generated using robust source classifiers transfer more effectively to other models, especially in the targeted setting, compared to those generated from standard classifiers.
The accuracy of zero-robust classifiers on robustified test sets decreases as the robustness parameter (ε) increases, similar to the known accuracy-robustness trade-off.
The results suggest that adversarial perturbations may appear non-semantic but are related to semantic features due to this entanglement.
papers.abstract: Neural networks trained on visual data are well-known to be vulnerable to often imperceptible adversarial perturbations. The reasons for this vulnerability are still being debated in the literature. Recently Ilyas et al. (2019) showed that this vulnerability arises, in part, because neural network classifiers rely on highly predictive but brittle "non-robust" features. In this paper we extend the work of Ilyas et al. by investigating the nature of the input patterns that give rise to these features. In particular, we hypothesize that in a neural network trained in a standard way, non-robust features respond to small, "non-semantic" patterns that are typically entangled with larger, robust patterns, known to be more human-interpretable, as opposed to solely responding to statistical artifacts in a dataset. Thus, adversarial examples can be formed via minimal perturbations to these small, entangled patterns. In addition, we demonstrate a corollary of our hypothesis: robust classifiers are more effective than standard (non-robust) ones as a source for generating transferable adversarial examples in both the untargeted and targeted settings. The results we present in this paper provide new insight into the nature of the non-robust features responsible for adversarial vulnerability of neural network classifiers.

papers.title: The Features at Convergence Theorem: a first-principles alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz for how networks learn representations
papers.research_question: Is there an alternative to the empirically-observed Neural Feature Ansatz conjecture, which can be derived from first principles?
papers.core_contribution: Derives the Features at Convergence Theorem (FACT) from first-order optimality conditions, providing a principled alternative to the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) that holds at convergence and captures feature learning phenomena.
papers.conclusion: FACT provides a first-principles alternative to the NFA, unifying theoretical optimality conditions with empirical feature learning, and captures global behaviors like grokking and phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
FACT, derived from first-order optimality, must hold at convergence and shows higher correlation with learned features than NFA and eNFA.
FACT captures feature learning phenomena such as grokking in modular arithmetic and phase transitions in sparse parity learning, similar to NFA.
FACT explains why NFA usually holds, as the two are proportional in many settings (e.g., modular arithmetic).
In degenerate settings, NFA can be nearly uncorrelated with the learned features while FACT still holds.
FACT-RFM achieves comparable performance to NFA-RFM on tabular data and synthetic tasks.
papers.limitation:
FACT has low correlation with neural feature matrices during most of training prior to interpolation, limiting its use for understanding feature evolution during training.
FACT requires non-zero weight decay, and it is unclear how to compute it in the zero weight-decay limit.
FACT-RFM can become unstable if continued iterations are performed after convergence, requiring early stopping in some settings.
future_direction: Derive a quantity with more stable correlation over training.
Understand the instability of FACT-RFM after convergence.
Compute FACT without weight decay via the neural tangent kernel.
papers.abstract: It is a central challenge in deep learning to understand how neural networks learn representations. A leading approach is the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) (Radhakrishnan et al. 2024), a conjectured mechanism for how feature learning occurs. Although the NFA is empirically validated, it is an educated guess and lacks a theoretical basis, and thus it is unclear when it might fail, and how to improve it. In this paper, we take a first-principles approach to understanding why this observation holds, and when it does not. We use first-order optimality conditions to derive the Features at Convergence Theorem (FACT), an alternative to the NFA that (a) obtains greater agreement with learned features at convergence, (b) explains why the NFA holds in most settings, and (c) captures essential feature learning phenomena in neural networks such as grokking behavior in modular arithmetic and phase transitions in learning sparse parities, similarly to the NFA. Thus, our results unify theoretical first-order optimality analyses of neural networks with the empirically-driven NFA literature, and provide a principled alternative that provably and empirically holds at convergence.

papers.title: Small Singular Values Matter: A Random Matrix Analysis of Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How is information stored in the singular-value spectra of transformer weight matrices, particularly in both large and small singular values?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that small singular values in transformer weight matrices carry important information and are crucial for model performance, which has implications for pruning and compression.
papers.conclusion: Small singular values are important for information storage in transformers and should not be neglected in pruning and compression.
papers.key_findings:
Small singular values in weight matrices deviate from Random Matrix Theory predictions, indicating learned structure.
Singular vectors corresponding to small singular values overlap with eigenvectors of activation covariance matrices, showing they capture important data directions.
Removing small singular values increases perplexity more than removing some larger ones, especially in non-square matrices.
Fine-tuning relies on small singular values; removing them after fine-tuning degrades performance significantly.
A linear random-matrix model explains how small singular values can carry information.
papers.abstract: This work analyzes singular-value spectra of weight matrices in pretrained transformer models to understand how information is stored at both ends of the spectrum. Using Random Matrix Theory (RMT) as a zero information hypothesis, we associate agreement with RMT as evidence of randomness and deviations as evidence for learning. Surprisingly, we observe pronounced departures from RMT not only among the largest singular values -- the usual outliers -- but also among the smallest ones. A comparison of the associated singular vectors with the eigenvectors of the activation covariance matrices shows that there is considerable overlap wherever RMT is violated. Thus, significant directions in the data are captured by small singular values and their vectors as well as by the large ones. We confirm this empirically: zeroing out the singular values that deviate from RMT raises language-model perplexity far more than removing values from the bulk, and after fine-tuning the smallest decile can be the third most influential part of the spectrum. To explain how vectors linked to small singular values can carry more information than those linked to larger values, we propose a linear random-matrix model. Our findings highlight the overlooked importance of the low end of the spectrum and provide theoretical and practical guidance for SVD-based pruning and compression of large language models.

papers.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
papers.research_question: Can we find and purify polysemantic neurons? How effective is PURE in disentangling representations compared to other approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PURE, a post-hoc method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into multiple pure virtual neurons by identifying the active circuit for each feature.
papers.conclusion: PURE turns polysemantic neurons into multiple purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits, resulting in more purified features than activation-based approaches and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons exist in ResNet models and can be disentangled into pure features using circuit identification.
PURE effectively disentangles representations, leading to more interpretable virtual neurons compared to activation-based clustering.
PURE attributions are more aligned with CLIP embedding distances than activations, indicating better neuron-specific disentanglement.
PURE performs close to DINOv2 in terms of cluster separation while being computationally more efficient than DINOv2-based clustering.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on foundational models (CLIP/DINOv2) as proxies for human interpretability, which may not perfectly align with human judgment.
PURE requires a partial backward pass for each neuron, making it computationally more demanding than activation-based methods.
future_direction: Evaluation in controlled settings or using human feedback for interpretability.
Ablation studies on clustering full circuits, different attribution methods, and clustering approaches.
Investigating advantages of purified units for XAI tools like concept-based explanations, concept discovery, probing, or model correction.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to study the role of individual neurons in Deep Neural Networks. Single neurons, however, have the capability to act polysemantically and encode for multiple (unrelated) features, which renders their interpretation difficult. We present a method for disentangling polysemanticity of any Deep Neural Network by decomposing a polysemantic neuron into multiple monosemantic "virtual" neurons. This is achieved by identifying the relevant sub-graph ("circuit") for each "pure" feature. We demonstrate how our approach allows us to find and disentangle various polysemantic units of ResNet models trained on ImageNet. While evaluating feature visualizations using CLIP, our method effectively disentangles representations, improving upon methods based on neuron activations. Our code is available at https://github.com/maxdreyer/PURE.

papers.title: Do Sparse Subnetworks Exhibit Cognitively Aligned Attention? Effects of Pruning on Saliency Map Fidelity, Sparsity, and Concept Coherence
papers.research_question: How does magnitude-based pruning followed by fine-tuning affect the interpretability of neural networks, specifically in terms of saliency map sparsity/faithfulness and concept coherence?
papers.core_contribution: Light-to-moderate pruning can improve saliency map sparsity and faithfulness while preserving distinct concepts, but aggressive pruning merges features and reduces concept coherence, indicating a trade-off between sparsity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning increases saliency sparsity and faithfulness and leads to more compact concept activations, suggesting pruning can improve post-hoc explanations in addition to compressing models.
papers.key_findings:
Light-to-moderate pruning (10-30%) increases saliency map sparsity and faithfulness.
Aggressive pruning (≥50%) reduces concept coherence and saliency map quality despite maintaining accuracy.
The effect of pruning on faithfulness is method-dependent: Vanilla Gradients benefits at light pruning, while Integrated Gradients requires heavier pruning.
Concept extraction shows moderate pruning preserves semantic purity, but heavy pruning leads to mixed, heterogeneous concepts.
Pruning can shape internal representations toward more human-aligned attention patterns, but excessive pruning undermines interpretability.
papers.abstract: Prior works have shown that neural networks can be heavily pruned while preserving performance, but the impact of pruning on model interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we investigate how magnitude-based pruning followed by fine-tuning affects both low-level saliency maps and high-level concept representations. Using a ResNet-18 trained on ImageNette, we compare post-hoc explanations from Vanilla Gradients (VG) and Integrated Gradients (IG) across pruning levels, evaluating sparsity and faithfulness. We further apply CRAFT-based concept extraction to track changes in semantic coherence of learned concepts. Our results show that light-to-moderate pruning improves saliency-map focus and faithfulness while retaining distinct, semantically meaningful concepts. In contrast, aggressive pruning merges heterogeneous features, reducing saliency map sparsity and concept coherence despite maintaining accuracy. These findings suggest that while pruning can shape internal representations toward more human-aligned attention patterns, excessive pruning undermines interpretability.

papers.title: Investigating the Effect of Network Pruning on Performance and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the impact of different pruning techniques on the classification performance and interpretability of GoogLeNet?
papers.core_contribution: Connection Sparsity pruning with iterative retraining achieves high compression with minimal accuracy loss, while the Mechanistic Interpretability Score (MIS) shows no correlation with pruning rate and may not reflect intuitive notions of interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Connection Sparsity pruning with iterative retraining offers a good balance between model compression and accuracy retention, but the MIS metric has limitations for assessing interpretability, especially for low-accuracy networks.
papers.key_findings:
Connection Sparsity pruning outperforms unstructured and structured pruning in preserving accuracy while significantly reducing network size.
Iterative pruning yields better accuracy than one-shot pruning but is computationally expensive.
There is no significant relationship between pruning rate and interpretability as measured by the MIS.
Networks with extremely low accuracy can still achieve high MIS scores, suggesting the metric may not align with understanding correct decisions.
The MIS score for the softmax layer was consistently low and showed no correlation with class-wise accuracy in pruned models.
papers.limitation:
The Mechanistic Interpretability Score (MIS) may not provide meaningful insights for networks with low accuracy and does not necessarily capture all aspects of decision-making clarity.
The MIS score for the softmax layer was consistently low and showed no correlation with class-wise accuracy, which is unexpected and suggests potential methodological issues.
future_direction: Future research should focus on developing more reliable interpretability metrics that consider both the clarity of the decision-making process and the quality of decisions made by the network.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are often over-parameterized for their tasks and can be compressed quite drastically by removing weights, a process called pruning. We investigate the impact of different pruning techniques on the classification performance and interpretability of GoogLeNet. We systematically apply unstructured and structured pruning, as well as connection sparsity (pruning of input weights) methods to the network and analyze the outcomes regarding the network's performance on the validation set of ImageNet. We also compare different retraining strategies, such as iterative pruning and one-shot pruning. We find that with sufficient retraining epochs, the performance of the networks can approximate the performance of the default GoogLeNet - and even surpass it in some cases. To assess interpretability, we employ the Mechanistic Interpretability Score (MIS) developed by Zimmermann et al. . Our experiments reveal that there is no significant relationship between interpretability and pruning rate when using MIS as a measure. Additionally, we observe that networks with extremely low accuracy can still achieve high MIS scores, suggesting that the MIS may not always align with intuitive notions of interpretability, such as understanding the basis of correct decisions.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in overlapping subsets of neurons across languages, with the extent of overlap varying by category, language proximity, and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, which may underpin their ability to generalize across languages and facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
There is significant cross-lingual overlap of neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
The overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and tends to be lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Neuron subsets are shared more between languages in the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with the amount of pre-training data for a language.
Overlap decreases in larger model architectures (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
future_direction: Artificially encouraging tighter neuron overlap might facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: Karolina Stanczak, Edoardo Ponti, Lucas Torroba Hennigen, Ryan Cotterell, Isabelle Augenstein. Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2022.

papers.title: Interpretability as Compression: Reconsidering SAE Explanations of Neural Activations with MDL-SAEs
papers.research_question: How can we use the Minimal Description Length principle to train and select Sparse Autoencoders that provide concise and interpretable explanations of neural activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an information-theoretic framework that views SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for neural activations, using the Minimal Description Length principle to select SAEs that provide concise and interpretable explanations, and introduces the property of independent additivity for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the MDL principle provides a theoretical motivation for SAE architectures and hyperparameters, and can help in creating principled evaluations for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be viewed as communication protocols for transmitting neural activations, and the MDL principle can be used to select SAEs that balance accuracy and conciseness.
Interpretability requires independent additivity, meaning features should be understandable separately.
On MNIST, MDL-SAEs find stroke-like features that are more interpretable and composable than features from very sparse or dense SAEs.
Optimizing for MDL can reduce undesirable feature splitting compared to optimizing for sparsity alone.
Hierarchical feature structures can lead to more efficient coding schemes and lower description length.
papers.limitation: The MDL principle is treated as a strategy for model selection: to choose a model out of a collection of multiple models. However, training multiple models with a hyperparameter sweep may be computationally expensive.
future_direction: Future work could look to include the entropy term in the loss function and optimise for it directly through either a straight-thought estimation approach or with a Bayesian prior.

Future work could explore to what extent variants in SAE architectures can decrease the MDL of communicated latent feature activations, and exploiting causal structure inherent in the data distribution may be important to efficient coding.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a useful tool for interpreting the internal representations of neural networks. However, naively optimising SAEs for reconstruction loss and sparsity results in a preference for SAEs that are extremely wide and sparse. We present an information-theoretic framework for interpreting SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for communicating explanations of neural activations. We appeal to the Minimal Description Length (MDL) principle to motivate explanations of activations which are both accurate and concise. We further argue that interpretable SAEs require an additional property, "independent additivity": features should be able to be understood separately. We demonstrate an example of applying our MDL-inspired framework by training SAEs on MNIST handwritten digits and find that SAE features representing significant line segments are optimal, as opposed to SAEs with features for memorised digits from the dataset or small digit fragments. We argue that using MDL rather than sparsity may avoid potential pitfalls with naively maximising sparsity such as undesirable feature splitting and that this framework naturally suggests new hierarchical SAE architectures which provide more concise explanations.

papers.title: Greedy-Gnorm: A Gradient Matrix Norm-Based Alternative to Attention Entropy for Head Pruning
papers.research_question: How can attention head pruning be improved by using dynamic, gradient-based importance scores that are recomputed after each pruning step, as opposed to static methods like attention entropy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Greedy-Gnorm, a dynamic attention head pruning algorithm that scores heads using the elementwise product of the ℓ2 norms of their Q/K/V gradient matrices and recomputes importance after each removal, outperforming static methods like attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: Greedy-Gnorm provides an effective dynamic gradient-based alternative to static head pruning, offering a foundation for integrating head pruning with broader model compression strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Greedy-Gnorm preserves model accuracy under substantial head removal, e.g., retaining ~20% of BERT heads while maintaining 90.08% accuracy (vs. 96.82% unpruned).
It consistently outperforms static attention entropy (AE) and random pruning baselines across BERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, and XLM-RoBERTa.
Pruning a head causes nonlocal gradient shifts, justifying the dynamic recomputation of importance scores.
The method achieves significant model size reduction (e.g., 22.5% for BERT) while maintaining competitive task performance.
Inverse pruning (removing highest-scoring heads first) causes rapid accuracy collapse, validating that the Gnorm score captures functional head importance.
papers.limitation:
Extra compute cost due to requiring a backward pass on a calibration set at each pruning step.
Assumes the calibration distribution is representative of deployment; mismatch can mis-rank heads.
Only prunes attention heads, not feedforward networks or tokens, so cannot remove all redundancy.
Gradients can be noisy for small batches or long contexts.
future_direction: Scaling to larger LLMs and additional architectures.
Extending to multi-dimensional pruning that jointly selects heads and feedforward network width.
Integrating Greedy-Gnorm with quantization and distillation for compounding compression.
Studying alternative scalar objectives (e.g., task loss vs. logit norms).
papers.abstract: Attention head pruning has emerged as an effective technique for transformer model compression, an increasingly important goal in the era of Green AI. However, existing pruning methods often rely on static importance scores, which fail to capture the evolving role of attention heads during iterative removal. We propose Greedy-Gradient norm (Greedy-Gnorm), a novel head pruning algorithm that dynamically recalculates head importance after each pruning step. Specifically, each head is scored by the elementwise product of the l2-norms of its Q/K/V gradient blocks, as estimated from a hold-out validation set and updated at every greedy iteration. This dynamic approach to scoring mitigates against stale rankings and better reflects gradient-informed importance as pruning progresses. Extensive experiments on BERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, and XLM-RoBERTa demonstrate that Greedy-Gnorm consistently preserves accuracy under substantial head removal, outperforming attention entropy. By effectively reducing model size while maintaining task performance, Greedy-Gnorm offers a promising step toward more energy-efficient transformer model deployment.

papers.title: Interpreting the Effects of Quantization on LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the effect of quantization on a model's confidence and calibration, the contribution of neurons to predictions, the number of 'dead neurons', and the redundancy of neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Quantization does not cause drastic changes in internal representations of LLMs, but its effects vary by model and task, supporting its reliability as a model compression technique.
papers.conclusion: The effect of quantization varies across datasets and models, but no major effect was observed that would discourage the use of quantization as a reliable approach for model deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Quantization does not lead to substantial change in model confidence and calibration.
The number of dead neurons remains largely unchanged with quantization.
Full-precision models have fewer salient neurons in smaller LLMs and more in larger ones, with quantization reversing this trend.
Neuron redundancy differs across models: Phi-2 full-precision has higher redundancy, while Llama-2-7B shows minor differences between quantized and full-precision versions.
The effect of quantization on model behavior is task- and model-dependent, but no major effect discourages its use.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limited experiments to specific quantization configurations, model sizes, and datasets.
Extreme quantizations such as 2-bit and 3-bit were not explored.
Generative tasks such as coding and summarization were not investigated.
future_direction: Explore extreme quantizations such as 2-bit and 3-bit.
Investigate generative tasks such as coding and summarization.
papers.abstract: Quantization offers a practical solution to deploy LLMs in resource-constraint environments. However, its impact on internal representations remains understudied, raising questions about the reliability of quantized models. In this study, we employ a range of interpretability techniques to investigate how quantization affects model and neuron behavior. We analyze multiple LLMs under 4-bit and 8-bit quantization. Our findings reveal that the impact of quantization on model calibration is generally minor. Analysis of neuron activations indicates that the number of dead neurons, i.e., those with activation values close to 0 across the dataset, remains consistent regardless of quantization. In terms of neuron contribution to predictions, we observe that smaller full precision models exhibit fewer salient neurons, whereas larger models tend to have more, with the exception of Llama-2-7B. The effect of quantization on neuron redundancy varies across models. Overall, our findings suggest that effect of quantization may vary by model and tasks, however, we did not observe any drastic change which may discourage the use of quantization as a reliable model compression technique.

papers.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons with a Null-Calibrated Polysemanticity Index and Causal Patch Interventions
papers.research_question: How can one systematically identify and quantify polysemantic neurons in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that combines geometric, categorical, and open-vocabulary semantic evidence to quantify when a neuron's top activations decompose into distinct, nameable concepts.
papers.conclusion: PSI provides a principled and practical tool for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks, and can be extended to benchmark across architectures and training regimes or to study interpretability-performance trade-offs.
papers.key_findings:
PSI robustly distinguishes real neuronal structure from chance, achieving an AUROC of approximately 0.99 when separating late-layer neurons from a null baseline.
Polysemanticity is an emergent property of network depth, with neurons in later layers (layer4) exhibiting significantly higher PSI scores than those in earlier layers (layer3).
Causal patch-swap interventions validate that the feature prototypes discovered by PSI are causally relevant to the neuron's function, with aligned patches increasing activation significantly more than various controls.
PSI rankings are robust to reasonable variations in hyperparameters, such as the number of top patches K, and the optimal number of clusters for decomposable neurons is typically 2 or 3.
The semantic distinctness score (D) is sensitive to the choice of text encoder, indicating that 'semantic distinctness' is relative to the conceptual ontology of the language model used.
papers.limitation:
The open-vocabulary distinctness score (D) is dependent on the chosen multimodal model (CLIP) and its conceptual vocabulary, making semantic distinctness relative to the model's 'conceptual lens'.
The methodology relies on specific choices such as top-K mining (which may miss polysemanticity at moderate activation levels) and K-means clustering (which assumes convex clusters and may not capture complex topological structures).
future_direction: Benchmarking PSI across different architectures and training regimes.
Using PSI as a regularizer to study the trade-off between interpretability and performance.
Extending the PSI approach to analyze neurons or attention heads in large language models (LLMs) or transformers.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often contain polysemantic neurons that respond to multiple, sometimes unrelated, features, complicating mechanistic interpretability. We introduce the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that quantifies when a neuron's top activations decompose into semantically distinct clusters. PSI multiplies three independently calibrated components: geometric cluster quality (S), alignment to labeled categories (Q), and open-vocabulary semantic distinctness via CLIP (D). On a pretrained ResNet-50 evaluated with Tiny-ImageNet images, PSI identifies neurons whose activation sets split into coherent, nameable prototypes, and reveals strong depth trends: later layers exhibit substantially higher PSI than earlier layers. We validate our approach with robustness checks (varying hyperparameters, random seeds, and cross-encoder text heads), breadth analyses (comparing class-only vs. open-vocabulary concepts), and causal patch-swap interventions. In particular, aligned patch replacements increase target-neuron activation significantly more than non-aligned, random, shuffled-position, or ablate-elsewhere controls. PSI thus offers a principled and practical lever for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks.

papers.title: What Is One Grain of Sand in the Desert? Analyzing Individual Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify and analyze individual neurons in deep NLP models? The paper also investigates how localized or distributed linguistic properties are, whether neurons are exclusive to certain properties, and how information distribution differs between NMT and NLM.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two methods for identifying and analyzing individual neurons in deep NLP models: a supervised Linguistic Correlation Analysis and an unsupervised Cross-model Correlation Analysis, and demonstrates their effectiveness through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes two methods for extracting salient neurons and demonstrates their accuracy through ablation experiments, with potential applications in model distillation and neural architecture search.
papers.key_findings:
Open class categories (e.g., verb, location) are more distributed across neurons than closed class categories (e.g., coordinating conjunction, determiner).
The model recognizes a hierarchy of linguistic properties and distributes neurons accordingly.
Important neurons extracted from Cross-model Correlation overlap with those from Linguistic Correlation (e.g., position neurons).
Ablating top neurons identified by Cross-model Correlation causes significant performance drop, validating the method.
Using only top neurons, classifiers can regain much of the performance, suggesting potential for model distillation.
future_direction: Applying the methods to model distillation and neural architecture search
Exploring recent architectures like Transformer and QRNN
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable evolution of deep neural networks in natural language processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. Previous work largely focused on what these models learn at the representation level. We break this analysis down further and study individual dimensions (neurons) in the vector representation learned by end-to-end neural models in NLP tasks. We propose two methods: Linguistic Correlation Analysis, based on a supervised method to extract the most relevant neurons with respect to an extrinsic task, and Cross-model Correlation Analysis, an unsupervised method to extract salient neurons w.r.t. the model itself. We evaluate the effectiveness of our techniques by ablating the identified neurons and reevaluating the network’s performance for two tasks: neural machine translation (NMT) and neural language modeling (NLM). We further present a comprehensive analysis of neurons with the aim to address the following questions: i) how localized or distributed are different linguistic properties in the models? ii) are certain neurons exclusive to some properties and not others? iii) is the information more or less distributed in NMT vs. NLM? and iv) how important are the neurons identified through the linguistic correlation method to the overall task? Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit (Dalvi et al. 2019a). This paper is a non-archived version of the paper published at AAAI (Dalvi et al. 2019b).

papers.title: Neuron Interaction Based Representation Composition for Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Can we better capture complex linguistic phenomena by composing the linguistic properties embedded in individual neurons through modeling strong neuron interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neuron interaction based representation composition method for neural machine translation, which uses bilinear pooling to model pairwise multiplicative interactions among neurons and extends it to incorporate first-order representations, leading to improved translation performance and better capture of syntactic and semantic information.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that modeling neuron interactions via bilinear pooling for representation composition improves translation performance and helps capture more linguistic information, and the approach is effective and efficient.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed neuron interaction based representation composition improves translation performance over the Transformer baseline on WMT14 English⇒German and English⇒French tasks.
The method helps the encoder capture more syntactic and semantic information, as shown by improved performance on probing tasks.
Multi-layer and multi-head composition are complementary, and combining them yields further gains.
Extended bilinear pooling (with first-order representations) outperforms bilinear pooling without first-order representations.
Low-rank approximation for bilinear pooling is effective, and even with a small rank constraint, the model outperforms the baseline.
future_direction: Exploring more neuron interaction based approaches for representation composition other than bilinear pooling.
Applying the model to a variety of network architectures such as BERT and LISA.
papers.abstract: Recent NLP studies reveal that substantial linguistic information can be attributed to single neurons, i.e., individual dimensions of the representation vectors. We hypothesize that modeling strong interactions among neurons helps to better capture complex information by composing the linguistic properties embedded in individual neurons. Starting from this intuition, we propose a novel approach to compose representations learned by different components in neural machine translation (e.g., multi-layer networks or multi-head attention), based on modeling strong interactions among neurons in the representation vectors. Specifically, we leverage bilinear pooling to model pairwise multiplicative interactions among individual neurons, and a low-rank approximation to make the model computationally feasible. We further propose extended bilinear pooling to incorporate first-order representations. Experiments on WMT14 English⇒German and English⇒French translation tasks show that our model consistently improves performances over the SOTA Transformer baseline. Further analyses demonstrate that our approach indeed captures more syntactic and semantic information as expected.

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Shift: Spurious Features Through the Lens of Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do spurious features affect model generalization, and can harmful spurious features be detected early during training by monitoring training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Spurious features can be benign or harmful depending on whether they are harder or easier to learn than core features. Harmful spurious features can be detected early by monitoring training dynamics using instance difficulty metrics like Prediction Depth.
papers.conclusion: Monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics can help identify harmful spurious features, saving time and computational costs and aiding in developing reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
Not all spurious features are harmful; they are harmful only if they are easier to learn than core features.
Prediction Depth (PD) can quantify feature difficulty and identify harmful spurious features during training.
Harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of a DNN's early layers.
Monitoring only accuracy during training is insufficient to detect spurious features; instance difficulty metrics are needed.
Theoretical connections exist between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like V-usable information.
future_direction: Develop intervention schemes to fix spurious feature problems early.
Unlearning spurious features from model representations.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are prone to learning spurious features that correlate with the label during training but are irrelevant to the learning problem. This hurts model generalization and poses problems when deploying them in safety-critical applications. This paper aims to better understand the effects of spurious features through the lens of the learning dynamics of the internal neurons during the training process. We make the following observations: (1) While previous works highlight the harmful effects of spurious features on the generalization ability of DNNs, we emphasize that not all spurious features are harmful. Spurious features can be "benign" or "harmful" depending on whether they are "harder" or "easier" to learn than the core features for a given model. This definition is model and dataset dependent. (2) We build upon this premise and use instance difficulty methods (like Prediction Depth (Baldock et al., 2021)) to quantify "easiness" for a given model and to identify this behavior during the training phase. (3) We empirically show that the harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of the DNN's early layers. In other words, easy features learned by the initial layers of a DNN early during the training can (potentially) hurt model generalization. We verify our claims on medical and vision datasets, both simulated and real, and justify the empirical success of our hypothesis by showing the theoretical connections between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like 𝒱-usable information (Ethayarajh et al., 2021). Lastly, our experiments show that monitoring only accuracy during training (as is common in machine learning pipelines) is insufficient to detect spurious features. We, therefore, highlight the need for monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics.

papers.title: When Reasoning Meets Compression: Understanding the Effects of LLMs Compression on Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How are the reasoning capabilities of large reasoning models (LRMs) affected by compression methods such as quantization, distillation, and pruning?
